docs.title: Problem 1 · A Caesar cipher that "moves"
docs.text:
Problem: an ordinary Caesar cipher shifts every letter by the same number of positions. Now change the rule: the 1st letter shifts by 13, the 2nd by 14, the 3rd by 15, and so on — each following letter shifts 1 more. Use the alphabet A–Z, wrapping around from Z to A. Encrypt SECURITY.

Think it through first

  • Number the letters: \(A=0,\ B=1,\ \ldots,\ Z=25\);
  • the i-th letter (i starting from 0) shifts by \(13+i\) positions;
  • if the result exceeds 25, subtract 26 (equivalent to \(\bmod 26\)).

Step-by-step calculation

Position Plaintext Value Shift Result Ciphertext 1 S 18 13 31 → 5 F 2 E 4 14 18 S 3 C 2 15 17 R 4 U 20 16 36 → 10 K 5 R 17 17 34 → 8 I 6 I 8 18 26 → 0 A 7 T 19 19 38 → 12 M 8 Y 24 20 44 → 18 S

The ciphertext is FSRKIAMS.

Why this is not an ordinary Caesar cipher: an ordinary Caesar cipher's "key" is a single number; here the shift is different at every position, which amounts to the key being a sequence of numbers \(13,14,15,\ldots\).

Common mistake: the 8th letter shifts by 20, not 13; \(Y(24)+20=44\), \(44-26=18\), which is S.

docs.title: Problem 2 · Running OTP backwards
docs.text:
Problem: the same 3-bit encoding: e=000, f=001, h=010, i=011, k=100, l=101, r=110, t=111. The OTP rule is \(C = P \oplus K\).

  1. Given the plaintext hike and the ciphertext left, find the key.
  2. Given the key keel and the ciphertext rile, find the plaintext.

Think it through first: XOR has a nice property — XOR the same thing twice and you get it back. So:

  • to find the key: \(K = P \oplus C\);
  • to find the plaintext: \(P = C \oplus K\).

docs.title: (1) Finding the key
docs.text:
Characters Bits Plaintext h i k e 010 011 100 000 Ciphertext l e f t 101 000 001 111 XOR t i l t 111 011 101 111

The key is tilt.

docs.title: (2) Finding the plaintext
docs.text:
Characters Bits Ciphertext r i l e 110 011 101 000 Key k e e l 100 000 000 101 XOR h i l l 010 011 101 101

The plaintext is hill.

In plain terms: OTP just "mixes" the plaintext and the key together; if you know two of them, you can "mix" the third one back out with XOR.

Common mistake: in the table i=011 and l=101, so do not read them off by row; the XOR result has to be mapped back in groups of 3 bits.

docs.title: Problem 3 · How long brute-force key search takes
docs.text:
Problem: suppose one machine can try \(2^{15}\) keys per second.

  1. An 80-bit key, worst case: how long does it take?
  2. A 50-bit key, average case: how long does it take?

Think it through first

  • an n-bit key has \(2^{n}\) possible values;
  • the worst case requires trying all of them;
  • on average only half are needed, that is \(2^{n-1}\);
  • the machine tries \(2^{15}\) per second, so the number of seconds = number of attempts ÷ \(2^{15}\).

docs.title: (1) 80-bit, worst case
docs.text:
\[ \frac{2^{80}}{2^{15}} = 2^{65}\ \text{seconds} \]

One year is about \(3.1536\times10^{7}\) seconds, so:

\[ \frac{2^{65}}{3.1536\times10^{7}} \approx 1.17\times10^{12}\ \text{years} \]

About 1.17 trillion years.

docs.title: (2) 50-bit, average case
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{2^{49}}{2^{15}} &= 2^{34}\ \text{seconds}\\ \frac{2^{34}}{3.1536\times10^{7}} &\approx 544\ \text{years} \end{aligned} \]

About 544 years.

In plain terms: each extra key bit doubles the work factor; 80-bit has 30 bits more than 50-bit, which is a factor of \(2^{30}\) more (about 1 billion times).

Common mistake: the average case uses \(2^{49}\), not \(2^{50}\); do not treat "seconds" as "years" directly.

docs.title: Problem 4 · Is this CTR formula sound?
docs.text:
Problem: normal CTR is \(C_{i} = P_{i} \oplus E(IV+i, K)\). Someone writes it as:

\[ C_i = P_i \oplus E(K, IV+i) \]

Note that this is \(E(\text{plaintext}, \text{key})\): K is put in the "plaintext" position, and IV+i becomes the "key" instead. Is this secure?

First look at the argument positions

  • Normal form: take IV+i as the plaintext and K as the key, encrypt to get a keystream, then XOR it with P_i;
  • This form: take K as the plaintext and IV+i as the key, encrypt something, then XOR.

The problem is that IV is public. So the "key" used for encryption is public, while the real key K is encrypted as the plaintext.

Attack: one known plaintext/ciphertext pair recovers K

  1. From \(C_{i} = P_{i} \oplus E(K, IV+i)\), XOR both sides with P_i: 
    1P_i ⊕ C_i = E(K, IV+i)
  2. The right-hand side is "encrypting K with the public IV+i as the key";
  3. The attacker knows the key IV+i, so she just decrypts: 
    1K = D(P_i ⊕ C_i, IV+i)
  4. Once she has K, every block can be decrypted: 
    1P_j = C_j ⊕ E(K, IV+j)

Conclusion: not secure. "K appears in the code" does not make it secure; what matters is whether K sits in the "plaintext" or the "key" position.

In plain terms: this is like treating the safe's key as the thing to be locked up, while the key to the lock is hanging on the door.

docs.title: Problem 5 · With a MAC and the key, can you build a new message?
docs.text:
Problem: CBC-MAC works like this:

\[ \begin{aligned} C_0 &= E(IV \oplus P_0, K)\\ C_i &= E(C_{i-1} \oplus P_i, K)\\ MAC &= C_{n-1} \end{aligned} \]

Now you know the MAC value X and you also know the key K, but not the original message. Can you assemble a new message whose MAC is still X? How many blocks are you free to choose?

Think it through first: the MAC is the final ciphertext block. The final block is determined by "the previous chaining value" and "the final plaintext block". Since you know K, you can work backwards: to make the final result X, what should the final plaintext block be?

Construction

  1. Choose the first \(n-1\) blocks \(P_0,\ldots,P_{n-2}\) freely;
  2. Compute \(C_{n-2}\) along the CBC chain;
  3. Set the final block to: 
    1P_{n-1} = D(X, K) ⊕ C_{n-2}
  4. Verify: 
    1MAC = E(P_{n-1} ⊕ C_{n-2}, K)
2    = E(D(X,K), K)
3    = X

Answer: yes. Apart from the final block, all earlier blocks can be chosen freely; the final block is uniquely determined by the prefix, the IV, K, and the target MAC.

In plain terms: a MAC is like "the final seal". If you know how the seal is made (K), you can arrange the earlier content however you like and then work backwards to the final block, so that the seal looks the same.

One more thing: this also shows that a MAC cannot resist forgery by someone who knows the key; it is not a digital signature.

docs.title: Problem 6 · Can CBC do random access?
docs.text:
Problem: CBC chains one block onto another. If you want to read only block i, what do you need? Compared with CTR, is it more trouble to change one block at random?

Reading one block

\[ P_i = D(C_i, K) \oplus C_{i-1} \]
  • You need C_i and the preceding block C_{i-1};
  • Block 0 has no "preceding block", so the IV takes its place.

So random reads are possible in CBC, you just have to fetch one extra ciphertext block.

Changing one block?

  • CBC: changing P_i changes C_i; C_i is also the input to the next block, so all later chaining values change. To keep the later plaintext intact, all ciphertext from i onward must be recomputed.
  • CTR: \(C_{i} = P_{i} \oplus E(IV+i, K)\), each block is independent; changing one block does not affect the others.

Conclusion: CBC suits sequential reads and writes; random reads are fine, but random writes/updates are expensive. CTR is better suited to random access.

In plain terms: CBC is like dominoes — knock one over and the rest fall with it; CTR is like a row of independent lamps — switching one off does not affect the others.

docs.title: Problem 7 · Replacing P1 with X in CBC
docs.text:
Problem: Alice sends 4 ciphertext blocks and the IV using CBC. Trudy can change the ciphertext in transit. If she knows P1, can she make the P1 that Bob decrypts become X?

First look at the decryption formula

\[ P_1 = D(C_1, K) \oplus C_0 \]

To make P1 become X, you need \(D(C_1,K) \oplus C_0'\) to equal X. D(C1,K) cannot be changed (C1 is untouched), but C0 can.

Method: set

\[ C_0' = C_0 \oplus P_1 \oplus X \]

Verification

\[ \begin{aligned} P_1' &= D(C_1, K) \oplus C_0'\\ &= D(C_1, K) \oplus C_0 \oplus P_1 \oplus X\\ &= P_1 \oplus P_1 \oplus X\\ &= X \end{aligned} \]

Side effect: since C0 changed, P0 also becomes garbled (\(P_0 = D(C_0',K) \oplus IV\)). If you only care about P1, that is acceptable.

Conclusion: CBC encryption does not provide integrity; if you know a plaintext block, you can change it in a targeted way.

In plain terms: CBC's first ciphertext block is like "seasoning" — the next block's plaintext is affected by it; change the seasoning a little and the next block tastes different.

docs.title: Problem 8 · The RSA homomorphism trick
docs.text:
Problem: Trudy obtains two ciphertexts encrypted with Alice's public key:

\[ \begin{aligned} C_0 &= M_0^e \bmod N\\ C_1 &= M_1^e \bmod N \end{aligned} \]

She does not know the private key or the plaintexts.

  1. Can she compute \((M_0\cdot M_1)^{e} \bmod N\)?
  2. What about \((M_0+M_1)^{e} \bmod N\)?
  3. What are the practical uses of fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)?

docs.title: (1) Multiplication
docs.text:
Simply multiply the two ciphertexts:

\[ C_0\cdot C_1 \equiv M_0^e\cdot M_1^e \equiv (M_0\cdot M_1)^e \pmod N \]

So the result is \(C_0\cdot C_1 \bmod N\).

In plain terms: RSA is like "doing multiplication while wearing gloves" — multiply the ciphertexts and, after decryption, you get exactly the product of the plaintexts.

docs.title: (2) Addition
docs.text: In general she cannot. RSA has only multiplicative homomorphism, not additive homomorphism; \(M_0^{e} + M_1^{e}\) is usually not equal to \((M_0+M_1)^{e}\). Special cases and exhaustive search aside, there is no comparable simple algebraic operation.

docs.title: (3) Uses of FHE
docs.text:
• Hand encrypted data to an untrusted server to compute on (statistics, machine learning, search);
  • The server never sees the plaintext and returns only the encrypted result;
  • Suits privacy-sensitive settings such as healthcare, finance, and genomics.

In one sentence: outsource the computation, but the data is never exposed.

docs.title: Problem 9 · Can a signature be "used backwards"?
docs.text: Problem: in the protocol, Alice signs M with her own private key and sends (M,S); Bob verifies with Alice's public key. Can Trudy make Bob accept a message that Alice never signed at all?

docs.title: (1) Is this forgery serious?
docs.text:
Trudy can:

  1. pick an R at will;
  2. compute \(N = \{R\}_{\text{Alice}}\) ("encrypting" R with Alice's public key);
  3. send (N, R) to Bob;
  4. Bob verifies \(\{R\}_{\text{Alice}} = N\), and so believes that N is a message signed by Alice.

What is this called: existential forgery. Trudy cannot freely choose a meaningful N, she only gets "the public-key encryption of R"; but Bob really does accept a message that Alice never signed.

Is it serious?: it is a security problem, not just a prank. If the system interprets N as a command, an amount, or a file name, real damage is possible; the "random message" is the only thing limiting its direct exploitation.

docs.title: (2) After switching to signing F(M), what must F satisfy?
docs.text:
The protocol becomes:

\[ S = [F(M)]_{\text{Alice}} \]

Bob verifies: [ {S}_{\text{Alice}} = F(M) ]

Trudy picks R, computes \(Y = \{R\}_{\text{Alice}}\), and now she has to find an M with \(F(M) = Y\) before she can send (M,R).

So F must be one-way (preimage-resistant):

Given Y, finding an M with \(F(M)=Y\) is computationally infeasible.

This way Trudy cannot turn an arbitrary Y into a valid message. In practice a collision-resistant hash (such as SHA-256) is used; one-wayness blocks this forgery, and collision resistance prevents "swapping the message".

In plain terms: originally what is signed is "the message itself", so an attacker can disguise the signature value as a message; once what is signed becomes "the message's fingerprint", the attacker cannot work backwards from a fingerprint to a message.

docs.title: Problem 10 · The "guaranteed" number for hash collisions
docs.text:
Problem: a hash outputs n bit, so there are at most \(2^{n}\) possible results. Now you want to guarantee finding 10 distinct colliding pairs of inputs (different pairs may share an input). What is the largest number of distinct inputs you need to try?

Think it through first: think of the \(2^{n}\) outputs as \(2^{n}\) buckets. Each input is thrown into one bucket; two inputs in the same bucket form one colliding pair.

Answer: \(2^{n} + 10\).

Why

  • If each bucket holds at most 1, you can place at most \(2^{n}\) inputs and there is not a single colliding pair;
  • Adding the \(2^{n}+1\)-th input must collide with an input in some bucket, giving the 1st pair;
  • after that, every extra "surplus" input adds at least one more pair;
  • so \(2^{n} + 10\) inputs give at least 10 pairs.

Why it cannot be fewer: with \(2^{n} + 9\), you can put 2 in each of 9 buckets and 1 in every other bucket; that gives only 9 pairs in total, not 10.

Common mistake: what is asked here is "guarantee" (worst case), not the "expected" \(2^{n/2}\) of a birthday attack.

In plain terms: it is not "try many times and probably collide", but "fill the drawers to a certain count and a duplicate is unavoidable".

docs.title: Problem 11 · How encryption and hashing differ
docs.text:
Problem: state the differences between encryption and hashing, at least three.

Dimension Encryption Hashing Key usually keyed an ordinary cryptographic hash is unkeyed Reversible can decrypt back to the plaintext one-way, cannot go back Output the ciphertext is usually about as long as the plaintext arbitrary length → fixed length Mapping should be reversible under a fixed key many-to-one, collisions are unavoidable Purpose confidentiality integrity / fingerprint / password storage

In plain terms

  • Encryption is like "a locked box": with the key you can open it, without the key you cannot;
  • a hash is like "a fingerprint": it can identify a person, but you cannot reconstruct the whole person from the fingerprint;
  • encryption must be reversible (otherwise the recipient cannot read it), and a hash must be irreversible (otherwise the fingerprint is meaningless).

In one sentence: encryption is "hiding something reversibly", and hashing is "an irreversible fingerprint".

docs.text: Problem Key point 1 shift \(13+i\); FSRKIAMS 2 \(K=P\oplus C\), \(P=C\oplus K\); tilt, hill 3 \(2^{65}\ \text{s} \approx 1.17\times10^{12}\ \text{years}\); \(2^{34}\ \text{s} \approx 544\ \text{years}\) 4 \(E(K, IV+i)\) uses the public IV as the key → K can be recovered 5 final block \(D(X,K)\oplus C_{n-2}\); the rest is free 6 CBC reads need the preceding block; changing a block requires recomputing the rest; CTR is independent 7 \(C_0'=C_0\oplus P_1\oplus X\) → \(P_1'=X\) 8 RSA is multiplicatively homomorphic; not additively; FHE for privacy-preserving computation 9 existential forgery; F must be one-way / collision resistant 10 \(2^{n}+10\); pigeonhole; \(2^{n}+9\) is not enough 11 key / reversible / fixed length / many-to-one

docs.title: Homework 2 · Reverse Engineering & Memory Safety
docs.text:
The question stems are desensitized restatements, not the original assignment text; the answers use plain language as much as possible and do not provide payloads that can be copied directly.

For review only; do not submit directly; the copyright of the course assignment and answers belongs to the instructor.

docs.title: Problem 1 · Two ways to "scan code"
docs.text:
Problem: there are two common approaches to disassembly: one scans byte by byte from beginning to end (linear), and one follows jumps/calls all the way (recursive). Answer three sub-questions:

  1. What are the pitfalls of scanning by following jumps?
  2. How do you fix that pitfall?
  3. What can a developer do to make reverse engineering more painful?

First, tell the two scanning methods apart

  • Linear disassembly: start from the first byte of the code section and decode one instruction after another downward, like reading a book from the first line to the last page.
  • Recursive disassembly: start from the entry point; whenever you hit jmp/call, follow the jump there and only decode the places that "really execute".

docs.title: (1) Pitfalls of scanning by following jumps
docs.text:
It can only follow direct jumps. Hitting an indirect jump is trouble, for example:

1jmp eax
2call [ebx+4]

What address is actually in eax? Static code analysis often cannot compute it (it may be a table filled in only at runtime, a virtual function, a callback). If you cannot compute it, you do not know where to go next, so you miss part of the code.

In one sentence: direct jumps can be followed, indirect jumps are easy to lose track of; code you lose track of is never disassembled.

docs.title: (2) How to fix it
docs.text:
• Combine them: run the recursive scan first; for regions that "fall in an executable section but are not covered by recursion", fill them in with a linear scan;
  • Compute it: constant propagation and emulated execution, to derive values such as eax as far as possible;
  • Find entries: use signatures/heuristics to recognize function starts and jump tables;
  • Run it: dynamic execution/instrumentation, to see which addresses are actually executed.

docs.title: (3) How to make reverse engineering more painful
docs.text:
• Code obfuscation: control flow flattening, opaque predicates, instruction replacement, so that the code "does not look like its original structure";
  • Packing/encryption: unpack only at runtime;
  • Anti-disassembly interference: embed data in the code section so that a linear scan treats data as instructions.

docs.title: Problem 2 · Are there really more malicious samples than normal software
docs.text:
Problem: some people say that the number of malicious samples now exceeds normal software, and signature databases can hardly hold them anymore.

  1. Is this claim reliable?
  2. If it really is like that, how should signature detection change?

docs.title: (1) Is it reliable
docs.text:
It depends on "how you count".

  • By sample/variant count: one malicious program can automatically generate a large number of polymorphic/metamorphic variants, and the count easily explodes; under this definition, "there are more malicious samples" is entirely possible.
  • By independent program/family count: the conclusion may be completely different, there are not that many "families".
  • Normal software also has many versions, but automated variants of malicious samples cost less.

So the sentence is reasonable under the definition of "counting by sample"; do not treat it as some specific global statistic conclusion.

docs.title: (2) How signature detection should change
docs.text:
A traditional signature is "a list of the bad characteristics". When bad samples outnumber good samples, the signature database explodes, and there will always be new variants that slip through.

Change direction: center on good software (allowlist)

  1. Trusted hash allowlist: only let reviewed executable files run;
  2. Isolate unknown files: not on the allowlist → sandbox/quarantine, instead of "let it through if there is no bad signature";
  3. The allowlist must resist tampering: sign it and authenticate updates, do not let the attacker modify the allowlist;
  4. Review process: review new versions first, then add them;
  5. Do not treat "approved" as "vulnerability-free": the allowlist only says "this is a program you approved", it does not mean it has no vulnerabilities; behavior monitoring and patch management are still needed.

In plain terms: rather than remembering "all the bad guys' faces", only let the "good guys on the list" in the door; people you do not recognize are first shown into a small room instead of being let straight into the office.

docs.title: Problem 3 · The pitfall of printf(name)
docs.text:
Problem: the following style of code:

1char name[64];
2scanf("%63s", name);
3printf(name);

User input is directly treated as a format string. Answer:

  1. What can the user do?
  2. Besides reading memory, can it also write?
  3. How do you fix it?

docs.title: (1) What the user can do
docs.text:
The first argument of printf is the "format string"; placeholders such as %s, %d, %x take the arguments after it. But here only one argument, name, is passed — where do the later arguments come from? — they are "grabbed" from the stack.

If the user inputs:

1%s%s%s

printf then treats three values on the stack as "string addresses" and prints out the memory there. The result may be:

  • leaking memory (data and addresses on the stack);
  • if some value is not a valid address, the program crashes.

%x also prints stack data in hexadecimal.

docs.title: (2) Can it be escalated from read to write
docs.text:
Yes, through %n.

%n prints nothing; instead it writes "the number of bytes output so far" to the address pointed to by the corresponding argument:

1int val;
2printf("blah %n blah\n", &val);
3// "blah " is 5 bytes, so val = 5

The attacker controls the format string, and therefore also controls the "arguments" that printf takes from the stack: they can specify the target address (return address, flag, GOT, etc.), and then use the output width to control the written value. So it escalates from "reading memory" to "arbitrary memory write", further hijacking control flow.

In plain terms: %s is "read out what is at the address", %n is "write a number to the address"; one peeks, one rewrites the books.

docs.title: (3) How to fix it
docs.text:
1. Hard-code the format string: printf("%s", name); — name is data, not a format;
  2. When formatting is not needed, use puts(name)/fputs;
  3. Never printf(user_input);
  4. Disable %n;
  5. Turn on compiler format-string warnings (-Wformat-security) and do code auditing.

Core: take the format string out of the user's hands.

docs.title: Problem 4 · The compiler itself is tampered with
docs.text:
Problem: a team audited the compiler source code and the account checker source code, and found no malicious code. But the compiler executable C0 they are using now has been contaminated and hides two rules:

  • when compiling "account checker" source code, insert a backdoor into the product;
  • when compiling "compiler" source code, insert these two rules into the new compiler.

They use C0 to compile C1, then use C1 to compile the account checker A1.

  1. Are C1 and A1 clean?
  2. Delete C0, use C1 to compile another C2 — does that solve it?
  3. If there is an independent trusted compiler T, how do you rebuild?

docs.title: (1) C1 and A1
docs.text:
• C1 contains the hidden rules: C0 recognizes "this is compiler source code" and inserts the two rules into C1;
  • A1 contains the backdoor: C1 recognizes "this is account checker source code" and inserts the backdoor into A1;
  • Both source files are clean, but the malicious behavior is "inherited" through the compiler.

In plain terms: it is not that something bad was written in the source code; the "translator" secretly adds a sentence while translating, so of course you cannot see it by checking the original text.

docs.title: (2) Delete C0, compile C2
docs.text:
It does not solve it. C1 already carries the rules; when it compiles compiler source code it inserts the same rules into C2; deleting C0 only deletes the "first generation" binary, later generations are still poisoned.

Key point: clean source code ≠ clean compiled binary; source code auditing cannot prove that the compiler is faithful.

docs.title: (3) Rebuild with a trusted T
docs.text:
1. In a trusted environment, use T to compile "compiler source code" → a clean C_clean;
  2. Use C_clean (or T directly) to compile "account checker source code" → a clean A;
  3. Replace all affected binaries, not just delete C0 or change the source code;
  4. Preferably use reproducible builds/diverse double-compiling to prevent contamination again.

Key point: swap out "the contaminated build products" and rebuild the toolchain from a trusted root.

docs.title: Problem 5 · Three login programs (overflow thinking)
docs.text:
Problem: there are three login programs; all take username/password from the command line and compare them with the secret in a file. The goal is to use an overflow to bypass the check and see a successful login. The three versions add different protections:

  • login1: no canary;
  • login2: fixed canary;
  • login3: canary computed from the username.

Below we only discuss the stack layout and the idea, and do not write out any payload that can be copied directly; the actual offsets must be confirmed with a debugger/disassembly.

The course also requires the username to start with your own student ID, and the contents of password.txt must not be used; not covered here.

docs.title: login1: consecutive fields
docs.text:
Layout: several fields are lined up next to each other on the stack:

1entered_name | entered_secret | stored_name | stored_secret

Idea:

  • fill only entered_name with the username, at a length that just does not go out of bounds;
  • the password starts writing from entered_secret and goes past its own buffer, overwriting the later stored_name and stored_secret;
  • the program writes a terminator at the end of each field; use filler to "push out" the extra characters;
  • at comparison time entered_name == stored_name, entered_secret == stored_secret, so the check passes.

In plain terms: you are not cracking the password, you are changing the "standard answer" to the copy you just wrote in.

docs.title: login2: fixed canary
docs.text:
Layout: fields interleaved with two tags:

1entered_name | stored_name | tag1 | stored_secret | tag2 | entered_secret
  • tag1 and tag2 are initially equal;
  • the username must overwrite stored_name, tag1, stored_secret, tag2, while keeping the two tags equal;
  • the password only has to fill entered_secret.

Idea:

  • use filler + the username/password you choose to overwrite the stored fields;
  • put the same value at both tag positions (the original fixed value, or the same non-zero byte);
  • this way the canary check passes and the comparison also passes.

In plain terms: the canary is a "fixed passphrase"; you just have to write the passphrase back in the right places and it will not notice.

docs.title: login3: dynamic canary
docs.text:
Layout: tags are both before and after the password buffer:

1expected_tag | entered_secret | boundary_tag | stored_secret | stored_name | entered_name
  • expected_tag is before the password buffer, so the password overflow cannot touch it;
  • boundary_tag is after entered_secret and will be overwritten by the password;
  • the program compares boundary_tag with expected_tag;
  • expected_tag is computed from the first few student-ID digits of the username, so it cannot be hard-coded.

Idea:

  1. fill entered_name with the username;
  2. the password starts at entered_secret and overwrites boundary_tag, stored_secret, stored_name in order;
  3. use the student-ID digits to compute the 6-byte tag G with the formula in the program;
  4. put G at the offset corresponding to boundary_tag, so that boundary_tag == expected_tag;
  5. put your username in stored_name and your password in stored_secret;
  6. the terminator lands at the end of stored_name; do not touch entered_name.

In plain terms: a dynamic canary is not "impossible to bypass", it is "the passphrase is different every time"; you have to understand how it is computed, then compute one yourself and put it back.

docs.title: Common pitfalls in the programming question
docs.text: Pitfall Explanation Copying the payload directly The offsets change with the compiler/stack layout, and are useless in another environment Username without student ID Course requirement; no points at all Using the contents of password.txt Forbidden by the problem; treated as the secret Ignoring the terminator The \0 at the end of each field changes the comparison Wrong canary position login2 needs the two tags to be equal; login3 needs the computed G Wrong file format Two lines: first line username, second line password

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text: Problem Key points 1 Recursion fears indirect jumps; linear + recursive are complementary; obfuscation/packing 2 Counting by variant → malware outnumbers; switch to allowlist + isolate unknown + signed updates 3 %s leaks, %n arbitrary write; printf("%s", name), ban %n 4 C1 carries the rules, A1 carries the backdoor; deleting C0 is useless; rebuild with trusted T and replace binaries 5 login1 consecutive fields; login2 fixed tag; login3 dynamic tag must be computed yourself

docs.title: How to use (the three-pass method)
docs.text:
Pass 1: build the framework (10–15 minutes per chapter) 1. Read the three sentences of the "Chapter thread"; 2. Go straight to the "Pre-exam quick-reference card" at the end; 3. Close the file and draw the chapter's knowledge structure on a blank sheet of paper (as much as you can).

Pass 2: nail down the mechanisms (60–90 minutes per chapter) 1. Read the "Key concepts" closely, and derive each formula yourself when you meet one; 2. Cover the worked-example solutions, do them yourself first, then compare; 3. Write the points you got wrong next to "Common mistakes" (or in your own error notebook).

Pass 3: self-test (30 minutes per chapter) 1. Cover the answers and do the "Self-test"; 2. For wrong answers, go back to the corresponding subsection of the key concepts; 3. The next day, review only the quick-reference card + the questions you got wrong.

30 minutes before the exam: review only each chapter's "quick-reference card" + "Common mistakes", plus the numbers table in §3.2 of the knowledge outline.

docs.title: One-sentence review per chapter
docs.text:
1. Chapter 1: security is CIA + threat model + cost trade-off; classical cryptography proves that "a large key space ≠ secure", and OTP is the theoretical upper bound but unusable.
  2. Chapter 2: stream ciphers emulate OTP, block ciphers rely on S-boxes; the mode determines multi-block security, MAC supplies integrity, and Grover only halves it.
  3. Chapter 3: RSA rests on the hardness of factoring, DH on the hardness of discrete log; signatures provide non-repudiation, PKI binds identity, and hashing comes before signing.
  4. Chapter 4: malware relies on propagation/disguise/backdoors; detection is an arms race of signatures vs behavior vs clustering; RE is "reading a program without source code".
  5. Chapter 5: a stack overflow overwrites ret to hijack control flow; NX/canary/ASLR each have limits; obfuscation only raises the cost of reverse engineering.
  6. Chapter 6: heap vulnerabilities are lifetime errors, format string/SQLi are "input treated as code/syntax"; side channels exploit physical leakage.
  7. Chapter 7: three authentication factors; passwords are weak because of user choice, salt raises the offline cost; the network is layered, and each layer has its corresponding attacks.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Content marked in the decks as "implementation not required" (AES round-function details, TEA code, RSA repeated-squaring details) is kept in these notes as "role/flow"; you are not required to memorize the code line by line.
  • In Chapter 7, the fraud/insult labels for biometrics are opposite to the usual false positive/negative; these notes record them as the "definition description" and mark them with ⚠.
  • In Chapter 2, \(2^{57}\) for 2DES and 112-bit for 3DES are two different things; these notes already distinguish them clearly, so do not mix them up in the exam.
  • If you want to expand a chapter into "30 practice questions + detailed solutions", or merge the 7 chapters into one printable PDF, you can keep building on top of the chapter contents.

docs.title: Chapter 1 · Introduction & Classical Cryptography · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w1/introduction-CSIT5730-26F.pdf, w1/classic-crypto.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 60 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.1, §2.2

Weight of this chapter: a high-frequency source for concept questions + threat modeling questions; classical crypto is usually only examined as multiple choice / fill-in / small computations, but the idea of OTP runs through all the cryptography that follows.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. Security is not a pile of tools, it is a way of thinking: first ask "which property do we want to protect (CIA)", then ask "who will attack how (threat model)", and only then work out "is it worth defending (cost/benefit)".
  2. Vulnerabilities come either from design or from implementation; design flaws cannot be solved by patching, implementation flaws can be patched but will be reused over and over.
  3. The value of classical crypto lies in establishing the vocabulary: Kerckhoffs's principle, a key space is not security, frequency analysis, and the fundamental contradiction between OTP's provable security and its "unusability".

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Concept discrimination What are the three elements of CIA? Given a scenario, decide which one is broken Memorize the definitions + prepare 2 examples per category Threat modeling Given a system (cloud / phone / enterprise intranet), write out attacker/capability/asset Apply the three-question template Principle application A certain design violates which Saltzer & Schroeder principle Remember 3 principles + be able to give examples Classical crypto computation Caesar decryption, key space, frequency analysis, OTP Be able to compute the bit count of 26!, be able to do XOR

docs.title: 1.1 The three CIA elements (must be able to say them without hesitation)
docs.text:
Element One-sentence definition Example of violation Where it reappears in this course Confidentiality Unauthorized parties cannot read the data eavesdropping, side channel, data breach, storing passwords in plaintext cryptography, side channel Integrity The data is accurate and has not been modified without authorization tampering with a transfer amount, ECB cut-and-paste, SQL injection modifying the database MAC (Message Authentication Code), signatures, hashing Availability Authorized users can access it whenever they need it SYN flood, worms, memory leaks, ransomware DoS, malware

Key understanding

  • CIA is not mutually exclusive: a single attack often breaks several at once. Ransomware = confidentiality (encryption) + availability (data unavailable); ARP spoofing = confidentiality (eavesdropping) + integrity (tamperable).
  • When analyzing any attack, the first sentence should be: "which one/ones of CIA does this break."
  • Authentication itself is not one of the CIA elements, but it is a prerequisite for achieving C/I/A; an authentication failure leads to unauthorized access.

docs.title: 1.2 Where do vulnerabilities come from (design vs. implementation)
docs.text:
Layer Concrete source Example Design Theoretical limitations the OTP key must be as long as the message → cannot be distributed at scale Lack of security features the protocol has no authentication → DH man-in-the-middle Side channels however correct the implementation, time/power/cache still leak the key Wrong threat model assuming "users will not modify the client" / "the cloud service provider is trusted" Wrong user model assuming users choose strong passwords and read certificate warnings Implementation Coding errors buffer overflow, UAF, format string Hardware errors Rowhammer, Spectre/Meltdown class Injected errors supply chain backdoor, malicious compiler (XcodeGhost) Failure to meet specifications the implementation is inconsistent with the protocol RFC, creating an opening

Where do attackers go to find vulnerabilities

  1. Find unknown vulnerabilities (0-day) — the hardest, but the most valuable;
  2. Buy 0-day — feasible, and it forms a black market;
  3. Reuse known vulnerabilities — the easiest: no patch applied, old systems, default configuration.

Exam point: "design flaws and implementation flaws are fixed in different ways". Design flaws require changing the protocol/architecture (possibly incompatible), an implementation flaw just needs a patch, but as long as unpatched machines remain it is still exploitable (the lesson of the Morris Worm).

docs.title: 1.3 The defender's three things
docs.text:
Concept Question it answers Output Security policy Which property do I want to enforce? a verifiable rule, e.g. "the password can only be stored on this machine", "a data pointer can only access the specified memory region" Risk assessment What assets do I have? Which is most critical? Who do I defend against first? asset inventory + risk ranking Threat model Who attacks? With what capability? What do they want to steal? the three elements attacker / capability / asset

Threat model template (use it directly in the exam)

  • System: ____
  • Attacker: ____ (e.g., co-tenant, service provider, network man-in-the-middle, malicious employee, the person who has the phone)
  • Capability: ____ (e.g., can share the CPU cache, can control the hypervisor, can send arbitrary packets, can physically touch the device)
  • Asset: ____ (e.g., private key, photos, password, transaction records)
  • Therefore what needs to be defended is: ____ (which one of CIA it corresponds to)

Cloud platform example (the slide example)

  • Attacker: the service provider, other cloud tenants.
  • Capability: the service provider can control everything (hypervisor, snapshots, scheduling); a co-tenant VM can share the same physical hardware with you (L1/L2 shared within a core, L3 shared across cores).
  • Asset: anything valuable (keys, data, models).
  • Conclusion: this is inherently a side channel threat model; beyond cryptography you must also consider physical/microarchitectural leakage.

Cost vs. benefit (defense is not "the stronger the better")

Option Advantage Cost Online kernel monitoring easy to deploy slows down the performance Offline formal verification no runtime overhead almost infeasible for a commercial OS

Exam point: if a scenario asks "why not use the strongest defense", the answer is usually cost, compatibility, performance, availability, not "it cannot be done".

docs.title: 1.4 Saltzer & Schroeder security design principles
docs.text:
The slides focus on 3 principles; you must be able to give "principle + explanation + example":

  1. Open design
    • Security depends only on the key, not on keeping the algorithm secret.
    • Rationale: once a secret algorithm leaks it is completely broken; in reality secrets do not stay secret; only openness lets peers find the weaknesses beforehand.
    • Counterexample: a home-grown "ancestral encryption algorithm", treating Base64 as encryption.
  2. Economy of mechanism
    • Simple interfaces, clean module boundaries, avoid global state.
    • Benefits: easier debugging, code audit, static/dynamic analysis, formal verification.
    • Counterexample: one function handles authentication, authorization, logging, and encryption at the same time — a huge attack surface that is hard to verify.
  3. Least privilege
    • Grant exactly "the minimum capability required to run".
    • Practice: grant nothing first, and add permissions one by one as errors appear; rather than granting root first and then taking it back.
    • Counterexample: using root for the database connection; an app demanding contacts + location + storage the moment it starts.

The complete classic list (supplementary; you can answer this if the exam asks "what else"): fail-safe defaults (deny by default), complete mediation (check every access), separation of privilege, least common mechanism, psychological acceptability (usability).

Note: the slides say "some of the rules may not be applicable nowadays"; when answering, do not be absolute — principles are a starting point for trade-offs, not dogma.

docs.title: 1.5 White hat ethics (for awareness)
docs.text:
• Test only on systems for which you have authorization; report found vulnerabilities through responsible disclosure; do not steal, do not damage, do not publish the details of unfixed issues.
  • The course has an ethics statement; "be a happy and ethic hacker".

docs.title: 2.1 Basic vocabulary and Kerckhoffs's principle
docs.text:
1plaintext P --encrypt E(K)--> ciphertext C --decrypt D(K)--> plaintext P
  • Symmetric: the same key encrypts and decrypts; public key: the public key encrypts, the private key decrypts (Chapter 3).
  • The intuition for security: computing P from C without the key is hard; with the key it is easy.
  • Kerckhoffs's principle: the security of a cryptosystem should depend only on the secrecy of the key, not on the secrecy of the algorithm.
  • This is "open design" embodied in cryptography.
  • Modern example: the AES algorithm is completely public, and security relies on the key.

docs.title: 2.2 Caesar cipher and frequency analysis
docs.text:
Caesar cipher: shift the whole alphabet by k. Encryption \(C = (P + k) \bmod 26\), decryption \(P = (C - k) \bmod 26\).

Example (the slide example): ciphertext CSYEVIXIVQMREXIH, known to be a Caesar cipher; find the plaintext. - Try k=4 (shift every letter back by 4): C→Y, S→O, Y→U, E→A, V→R, I→E, X→T, ... - Result: YOU ARE TERMINATED. - Why so fast? Because Caesar has only 25 nonzero keys, so exhaustive key search is enough.

General simple substitution: an arbitrary permutation of letters, key space 26!. - \(26! = 403{,}291{,}461{,}126{,}605{,}635{,}584{,}000{,}000 \approx 4.03\times10^{26}\) - \(\log_2(26!) \approx 88.4\), i.e. > \(2^{88}\), exhaustive search is infeasible. - But frequency analysis breaks it: 1. Count the ciphertext letter frequencies; 2. Align them with the English distribution (e/t/a are the most common; slide example: {h,l,r} → {t,a,e}); 3. Verify with high-frequency words / pattern words (e.g. gur → the); 4. Iterate the substitution and expand step by step.

Core conclusion: a large key space ≠ security. As long as a "shortcut" attack exists, it is insecure.

docs.title: 2.3 An operational definition of "secure"
docs.text:
• If the best known attack is exhaustive search, the system is called secure;
  • If any shortcut smarter than exhaustive search exists, it is insecure;
  • But "exhaustive search" itself must also be infeasible — DES's 56-bit is the counterexample (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 2.4 One-time pad (OTP)
docs.text:
Mechanism: \(C = P \oplus K\), \(P = C \oplus K\) (XOR is self-inverse: XOR the same value twice and you get the original back).

Slide example (3-bit encoding e=000, h=001, i=010, k=011, l=100, r=101, s=110, t=111):

Plaintext Key Ciphertext Characters h e i l h i t l e r — (keystream) s r l h s s t h s r Bits 001 000 010 100 001 010 111 100 000 101 111 101 110 101 111 100 000 101 110 000 110 101 100 001 110 110 111 001 110 101

Why it is provably secure

  • Every bit of the key is equally likely at random ⇒ for any plaintext, the ciphertext is uniformly distributed over the ciphertext space ⇒ the ciphertext carries no information about the plaintext.
  • Formal statement: \(P(C=c \mid P=p_1) = P(C=c \mid P=p_2)\) holds for any p1, p2.

The three required conditions (violating any one breaks it)

  1. The key is truly random;
  2. The key is used only once;
  3. The key is as long as the message.

Fatal problem: the key is as long as the message and must be distributed securely — "so why not just transmit the key?" This is the key distribution problem, and it is exactly the problem public key cryptography has to solve.

Real-world case VENONA: Soviet spies used OTP, but the "one-time" pads were reused, so a large number of ciphertexts could be broken by correlation analysis.

Two-time pad attack (must know)

If \(C_{1} = P_{1} \oplus K\), \(C_{2} = P_{2} \oplus K\), then:

\[ C_1 \oplus C_2 = P_1 \oplus P_2 \]
  • If P1 is known, then \(P_{2} = C_{1} \oplus C_{2} \oplus P_{1}\);
  • If both P1 and P2 are English, then \(P_{1} \oplus P_{2}\) can be guessed word by word with "crib-dragging".

4-bit mini example: P1=1010, K=0110 → C1=1100; P2=0011 → C2=0101. \(C_{1}\oplus C_{2} = 1001 = P_{1}\oplus P_{2}\); given P1=1010 ⇒ \(P_{2} = 1001\oplus 1010 = 0011\).

docs.title: 2.5 Codebook cipher
docs.text:
• A codebook maps words/phrases to codewords (the Zimmerman Telegram).
  • Additive: stack another "book of random numbers" on top; send the ciphertext + the additive position (the position is not secret); the receiver subtracts the additives first, then looks up the codebook.
  • Purpose: the same word is encoded differently each time, resisting frequency analysis.
  • Modern connection: a block cipher is an electronic codebook (ECB mode), see Chapter 2.

docs.title: 2.6 The three legacies of classical cryptography
docs.text:
1. Kerckhoffs's principle: the algorithm is public, the key is secret.
  2. Security = resistance to the strongest known attack, not "it looks random".
  3. OTP is the theoretical upper bound: provably secure, but key distribution is infeasible → all the cryptography that follows is "approximating the effect of OTP with a short key".

docs.title: Example 1: Caesar decryption (5 points)
docs.text:
Question: the ciphertext CSYEVIXIVQMREXIH was produced by a Caesar cipher; find the plaintext and the key.

Solution: - Try all 25 keys, or observe the high frequencies: I and V appear several times, so guess I→E (shift by 4). - Solve with \(P = C-4\): YOU ARE TERMINATED. - Key k=4 (+4 when encrypting).

Scoring points: write the formula \(P=(C-k) \bmod 26\); state that "Caesar has only 25 keys, so it can be exhaustively searched".

docs.title: Example 2: Key space and security (5 points)
docs.text:
Question: a general simple substitution has 26! keys, why is it still insecure?

Solution: - 26! ≈ \(2^{88}\)·⁴, exhaustive search really is infeasible; - but a simple substitution preserves the letter frequency distribution, so frequency analysis + pattern words can recover the mapping step by step; - therefore the "best attack" is not exhaustive search but frequency analysis → by definition it is insecure.

Scoring points: distinguish "a large key space" from "a strong ability to resist attack".

docs.title: Example 3: OTP reuse (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: two messages are encrypted with the same OTP key, giving C1 and C2. The attacker knows P1; how is P2 recovered? State what condition is required.

Solution: - \(C_{1}\oplus C_{2} = (P_{1}\oplus K)\oplus (P_{2}\oplus K) = P_{1}\oplus P_{2}\); - \(P_{2} = C_{1}\oplus C_{2}\oplus P_{1}\); - Condition: the same key was used twice (violating OTP condition 2); if P1 is unknown but is natural language, crib-dragging can be used to guess it.

docs.title: Example 4: Threat modeling (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: a "cloud photo backup app" encrypts the user's photos in the app before uploading. Build a threat model and point out the two attacks that most need defending against.

Reference answer: - Attacker: ① the cloud service provider (can control the VM, take snapshots, read memory); ② a co-tenant (shared CPU cache); ③ the person who has the user's phone; ④ a network man-in-the-middle. - Capability: the service provider can read VM memory/disk; a co-tenant can measure cache timing; the phone holder can unlock / install a malicious app; the man-in-the-middle can tamper with the traffic. - Asset: the photo contents, the encryption key, the account credentials. - Most in need of defense: ① the service provider/co-tenant obtaining the key through a side channel (corresponding to confidentiality); ② the client key being stolen by a malicious app / the phone holder (corresponding to confidentiality + authentication). - Defense direction: end-to-end encryption, the key never leaves the secure area, constant-time implementation, device authentication.

Scoring points: all three elements present; attacks correspond to assets; defenses correspond to attacks.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes (where marks are most easily lost in the exam)
docs.text: Wrong statement Correct understanding "CIA is three parallel security goals, and every system must satisfy all of them 100%" the three need trade-offs; different systems have different priorities (an ATM weights integrity more, a video site weights availability more) "A large key space means secure" you also have to check whether a shortcut attack exists; the 26! simple substitution is broken by frequency analysis "OTP is secure as long as the key is random" it must also be used only once and as long as the message "Kerckhoffs's principle requires the algorithm to be public" it says "security should not depend on keeping the algorithm secret"; open design is a recommended practice, not a mathematical requirement "A threat model = risk analysis" a threat model answers "who, with what capability, steals what"; risk analysis answers "how important the assets are, who to defend against first" "Design flaws and implementation flaws can both be patched" design flaws usually require changing the protocol/architecture and may be incompatible; implementation flaws can be patched but the machines already in the field are still at risk "A white hat can test whatever they like" authorization is required; unauthorized testing is an attack

docs.title: 5. Self-test (do it first, then look at the answers)
docs.text:
1. Define CIA in one sentence each, and give one attack from later in this course for each.
  2. Give three examples each of the "design causes" and the "implementation causes" of vulnerabilities.
  3. What are the three elements of a threat model? Write one out for a "campus course registration system".
  4. What problem does each of Saltzer & Schroeder's open design, economy of mechanism, and least privilege solve?
  5. Why is "open design" actually more secure? Give a counterexample.
  6. How large is the Caesar cipher's key space? Why is it insecure?
  7. Roughly how many bits is 26!? What does this number show, and what does it not show?
  8. What are the three conditions for OTP? What happens if any one of them is violated?
  9. Two ciphertexts C1 and C2 are encrypted with the same OTP key; write the quantity the attacker can compute directly.
  10. Why is OTP said to be "provably secure but unusable"? What is its relation to modern stream ciphers?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. Confidentiality (side channel stealing the key), integrity (ECB cut-and-paste), availability (SYN flood).
  2. Design: OTP key distribution, protocol without authentication, wrong threat model; implementation: buffer overflow, UAF, format string.
  3. Attacker (student / outside hacker / internal administrator), Capability (has a student ID and can log in / can access the intranet / can touch the database), Asset (grades, personal information, course registration records).
  4. Open design: avoids "the whole system collapsing the moment a secret algorithm leaks"; Economy: lowers the cost of audit and verification; Least privilege: limits the impact scope after a vulnerability is exploited.
  5. Openness lets more people review and find weaknesses beforehand; counterexample: a home-grown private encryption algorithm — once it is reversed there is no security left, and nobody helps you find vulnerabilities.
  6. 25 nonzero keys (or 26 including 0); it can be exhaustively searched, and the frequency distribution is preserved.
  7. ≈ \(2^{88}\)·⁴; it shows that exhaustive search is infeasible; it does not show resistance to shortcut attacks such as frequency analysis.
  8. Truly random, used only once, as long as the message; violating them leads respectively to predictability, a two-time pad, and infeasible key distribution.
  9. \(C_{1}\oplus C_{2} = P_{1}\oplus P_{2}\).
  10. Because information-theoretically the ciphertext leaks nothing about the plaintext, but the key must be as long as the message and be distributed securely; a stream cipher uses a short key to generate a pseudorandom keystream to "simulate" OTP.

docs.title: 6. Pre-exam quick-reference card
docs.text: Point Content CIA Confidentiality / Integrity / Availability Source of vulnerabilities design (theoretical limitations, missing features, side channels, wrong threat/user model) / implementation (coding, hardware, injected, non-compliant) The defender's three things policy → risk assessment → threat model The threat model's three questions who / capability / what asset The three principles open design, economy of mechanism, least privilege Kerckhoffs security depends only on the key, not on keeping the algorithm secret Caesar 25 keys, exhaustively searchable; \(P=(C-k) \bmod 26\) Simple substitution 26! ≈ \(2^{88}\)·⁴, but frequency analysis breaks it OTP \(C=P\oplus K\); random, once, same length; two-time pad → \(C_{1}\oplus C_{2}=P_{1}\oplus P_{2}\) Definition of security best attack = exhaustive search → secure; a shortcut exists → insecure Classical legacy Kerckhoffs, resistance to the strongest attack, OTP as the theoretical upper bound

docs.title: Chapter 2 · Symmetric Key Cryptography · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w2/Symmetric-Key-Crypto.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 90 minutes + worked examples 40 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.3

Weight of this chapter: the main battleground for crypto computation and mechanism questions. DES/AES parameters, the Feistel formulas, the three modes, MAC, and Grover — at least one of them is almost certain to be examined.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. Stream ciphers use a short key "stretched" into a pseudorandom keystream — in essence a simulated OTP; block ciphers iterate a round function over fixed-sized blocks — in essence an electronic codebook.
  2. The security of a block cipher comes from its non-linear S-boxes; DES relies on 8 S-boxes, AES on ByteSub + MixColumn.
  3. Encryption only provides confidentiality, not integrity; multi-block data must rely on modes, and integrity must rely on a MAC; quantum computing only "halves" the strength of a symmetric key (Grover).

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Parameter fill-in Block, key, and round counts for DES/AES/3DES/TEA Memorize the §7 quick-reference table Mechanism derivation Write one Feistel round, one A5/1 step, the CBC/CTR encryption equations Be able to derive the formulas, not just memorize the conclusions Mode comparison Pros and cons of ECB/CBC/CTR, and when to use them Tie it together with "does the same plaintext block give the same ciphertext?" Computation 2DES meet-in-the-middle, Grover, MAC overhead Remember \(2^{57}\), \(2^{n/2}\), 1.5× Design question Why does 3DES use EDE? Why does MAC use a different key? Answer "backward compatible / avoid MITM / avoid key reuse"

docs.title: 1.1 Role
docs.text:
• The key is relatively short (e.g., 128 bit), but the algorithm stretches it into a keystream as long as the message.
  • Encryption: \(C_i = P_i \oplus KS_i\); decryption likewise. Used exactly like a one-time pad (OTP).
  • Advantages: extremely efficient in hardware, small memory footprint, suitable for voice/embedded.
  • Disadvantages: slow in software; on modern CPUs block ciphers (especially AES-NI) are faster.
  • Representatives: A5/1 (GSM), RC4.

docs.title: 1.2 A5/1 (hardware stream cipher) ★
docs.text:
Structure

Register Length Stepping taps Notes X 19 bit \(t = x_{13} \oplus x_{16} \oplus x_{17} \oplus x_{18}\) Shift right, the new bit enters x0 Y 22 bit \(t = y_{20} \oplus y_{21}\) Shift right, the new bit enters y0 Z 23 bit \(t = z_{7} \oplus z_{20} \oplus z_{21} \oplus z_{22}\) Shift right, the new bit enters z0

Each step

  1. Take the clocking bits: \(m = \mathrm{maj}(x_8, y_{10}, z_{10})\) (majority of three).
  2. If \(x_8 = m\), X steps; if \(y_{10} = m\), Y steps; if \(z_{10} = m\), Z steps (two or three registers may step at the same time).
  3. Output the keystream bit: \(x_{18} \oplus y_{21} \oplus z_{22}\).

Majority example: \(\mathrm{maj}(0,0,1)=0\), \(\mathrm{maj}(1,1,0)=1\), \(\mathrm{maj}(1,0,1)=1\).

Slide example: if \(m = \mathrm{maj}(1,0,1) = 1\), then X steps, Y does not step, and Z steps; the output bit = XOR of the rightmost bits of the three registers (1 in this example).

Design trade-off: shift registers are extremely cheap in hardware; but bit-by-bit software implementations are very slow. GSM used it because of the hardware constraints of the time.

Note: A5/1 itself has known attacks (not covered in the slides), so do not treat it as a synonym for "secure"; if the exam asks "why is it rarely used now", answer "software efficiency + known weaknesses".

docs.title: 1.3 RC4 (software stream cipher) ★
docs.text:
Core: a 256-byte permutation table S that is "self-modifying" with the key; each step outputs 1 byte.

KSA (key scheduling algorithm, initialization)

1for i = 0..255:
2    S[i] = i
3    K[i] = key[i mod N]      # N = number of key bytes, any length
4j = 0
5for i = 0..255:
6    j = (j + S[i] + K[i]) mod 256
7    swap(S[i], S[j])
8i = j = 0

PRGA (pseudo-random generation algorithm)

1i = (i + 1) mod 256
2j = (j + S[i]) mod 256
3swap(S[i], S[j])
4t = (S[i] + S[j]) mod 256
5keystreamByte = S[t]
  • Each step produces 1 byte (A5/1 produces 1 bit per step).
  • The first 256 bytes must be discarded: otherwise the initial output is biased and an attack exists (stated in the slides).
  • Naming trap: RC5 is a block cipher, not an upgrade of RC4.

docs.title: 2.1 Feistel cipher ★★
docs.text:
A Feistel cipher is not a specific algorithm but a framework: DES, Blowfish, RC5, TEA, and Twofish are all instances or related structures.

Encryption (P = (L0, R0))

\[ \begin{aligned} L_{i+1} &= R_i \\ R_{i+1} &= L_i \oplus F(R_i, K_i),\quad i = 0,\dots,n \\ C &= (R_{n+1}, L_{n+1}) \end{aligned} \]

(the halves are swapped at the end)

Decryption (start from \(C = (R_{n+1}, L_{n+1})\), subkeys in reverse order)

\[ \begin{aligned} R_{i-1} &= L_i \\ L_{i-1} &= R_i \oplus F(L_i, K_{i-1}) \\ P &= (L_0, R_0) \end{aligned} \]

Two points you must understand

  1. Decryption works for any F: every round is a reversible linear/XOR operation, so F need not be invertible.
  2. Security holds only for certain F: if \(F = 0\), each round is just a swap of the halves, two rounds undo it, and it is completely insecure.

One-round example: \(L_0=0110\), \(R_0=1001\), \(K=1111\), \(F(R,K)=R\oplus K\).

  • \(L_1 = R_0 = 1001\)
  • \(R_{1} = L_{0} \oplus F(R_{0},K) = 0110 \oplus (1001\oplus 1111) = 0110 \oplus 0110 = 0000\)
  • \(C = (R_1, L_1) = (0000, 1001)\)

Decryption check: \(R_0 = L_1 = 1001\); \(L_{0} = R_{1} \oplus F(L_{1},K) = 0000 \oplus (1001\oplus 1111) = 0110\). The plaintext is recovered.

docs.title: 2.2 DES ★★
docs.text:
Parameter Value Block length 64 bit Key length 56 bit (64 bit, of which 8 are parity bits) Rounds 16 Subkey used each round 48 bit Structure Feistel Source of security 8 S-boxes (6 bit → 4 bit)

One round (memorize the order)

1R (32 bit)
2  → expansion permutation E → 48 bits
3  → XOR with subkey Ki (48 bits)
4  → 8 S-boxes (each 6→4) → 32 bits
5  → P-box permutation → 32 bits
6  → XOR with L
7  → swap left and right

One round of DES: the 32-bit R is expanded to 48 bit, XORed with the 48-bit subkey, passed through eight S-boxes back to 32 bit, then permuted by the P-box and XORed with L; the right side shows subkey generation.

  • Expansion permutation E: 32 → 48 bit; by repeating edge bits it splits the data into 8 groups of 6 bit each.
  • S-box: the only non-linear component. Input 6 bit: the outer 2 bit select the row (0–3), the middle 4 bit select the column (0–15); output 4 bit. The DES S-boxes are carefully designed to resist differential/linear cryptanalysis → this is mainly where the security of DES comes from.
  • P-box: further permutes the 32-bit output, providing diffusion.
  • Subkey generation: the 56-bit key is split into two 28-bit halves, each cyclically left-shifted every round, then compressed to select 48 bit.
  • Initial permutation IP / final permutation FP: provide no security at all, they are just a historical design; software implementations often omit them.

Expansion permutation E: eight 6-bit outputs (input bit numbers 0–31)

Group 6-bit output (input bit numbers) 1 31, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 2 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 3 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 4 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 5 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 6 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 7 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 8 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 0

Adjacent groups share two edge bits, so 32 bit are "stretched" into 48 bit; this is not arbitrary repetition — it makes every S-box input cross the original 4-bit boundary and improves diffusion.

P-box (32 → 32)

Output bits Input bit numbers 0–15 15, 6, 19, 20, 28, 11, 27, 16, 0, 14, 22, 25, 4, 17, 30, 9 16–31 1, 7, 23, 13, 31, 26, 2, 8, 18, 12, 29, 5, 21, 10, 3, 24

The P-box scatters each S-box output bit to a different S-box in the next round, preventing one group from permanently influencing the same group.

Decryption: DES decryption uses the same Feistel network, but applies the 16 subkeys in reverse order \(K_{16},K_{15},\dots,K_1\); IP and FP are inverse permutations.

Cracking history (memorize the numbers)

  • 1998, the EFF DES Cracker: cost < $250,000, cracked in < 3 days.
  • 1999, distributed.net: using the idle time of many machines, 22 hours and 15 minutes.
  • Conclusion: a 56-bit key is too small, exhaustive search is feasible; DES is no longer secure.

docs.title: 2.3 3DES (Triple DES) ★
docs.text:
Structure: \(C = E(D(E(P,K_1),K_2),K_1)\), i.e., EDE, two keys, effective strength 112 bit.

Why EDE instead of EEE?

  • Backward compatible: when \(K_1 = K_2 = K\), \(E(D(E(P,K),K),K) = E(P,K)\), which degrades to ordinary DES.
  • This way old systems being upgraded can interoperate in single-key mode.

Why not double encryption \(E(E(P,K_1),K_2)\)?

  • Double encryption nominally has 112-bit strength, but there is a meet-in-the-middle (MITM) attack:
  • For each K1 compute \(E_{K_{1}}(P)\) and store it (about \(2^{56}\));
  • For each K2 compute \(D_{K_{2}}(C)\) and look for a match (about \(2^{56}\));
  • Total time/space about \(2^{56}\) each, together about \(2^{57}\), not \(2^{112}\).
  • The EDE structure of 3DES (outer E with K1, inner D with K2) cannot be attacked by this simple meet-in-the-middle directly, so it keeps about 112-bit strength.

⚠ Common mistake: the "\(2^{112}\) → \(2^{57}\)" in the slides refers to double encryption, 2DES; do not take \(2^{57}\) as the effective strength of 3DES. The two-key version of 3DES is about 112 bit.

Three-key 3DES: E(D(E(P,K1),K2),K3), strength about 168 bit (the slides only cover the two-key version).

docs.title: 2.4 AES ★★
docs.text:
Parameter Value Block length 128 bit (16 bytes, 4×4 byte array) Key length 128 / 192 / 256 bit Rounds 10 / 12 / 14 (matching the keys above) Structure Not a Feistel cipher (SPN type)

The 4 operations in each round (the order must not be wrong)

  1. ByteSub (SubBytes): byte-by-byte S-box lookup, the only non-linear layer; no fixed point (\(S(a) \neq a\)), and an inverse table is needed for decryption.
  2. ShiftRow (ShiftRows): row 0 is not shifted, row 1 is shifted by 1 byte, row 2 by 2, row 3 by 3; the purpose is to mix the columns, avoiding the columns being encrypted independently.
  3. MixColumn (MixColumns): each column is multiplied on the left by an invertible matrix (over GF(\(2^{8}\))), implemented as a lookup table; it provides diffusion within a column.
  4. AddRoundKey: XOR the subkey with the block (the only "key injection" step).

Why AES is popular

  • Efficient on both 8-bit / 32-bit CPUs; small code and memory footprint.
  • Hardware instructions AES-NI (AESENC / AESDEC) exist, and software is fast too.
  • Avalanche effect: one bit difference in the plaintext → a big change in the ciphertext.

The slides state explicitly: you are NOT required to remember AES implementation details, but you must be able to explain clearly what the four operations do, and "why it is not a Feistel cipher" (AES applies substitution-permutation to the whole block each round, instead of only handling half of it).

docs.title: 2.5 TEA (Tiny Encryption Algorithm)
docs.text:
Parameter Value Block 64 bit Key 128 bit Rounds Variable, 32 rounds is considered secure Constant \(\delta = \texttt{0x9e3779b9}\) (golden ratio) Characteristics "Weak" round function + many rounds; "almost Feistel" (uses +/- instead of pure XOR)

Weakness: equivalent keys exist (4 different keys that all give the same ciphertext), lowering the effective strength from \(2^{128}\) to about \(2^{126}\); there are also X-box type attacks. The slides do not require you to remember the implementation.

docs.title: 2.6 Linear cryptanalysis ★
docs.text:
• The only non-linear component of a block cipher is the S-box; the attack idea is to approximate the S-box with linear equations.
  • For a given S-box, measure the probability that a linear relation between input and output bits holds:
  • \(y_1 = x_1\) holds with probability 3/4;
  • \(y_{0} = x_{0} \oplus x_{2} \oplus 1\) holds with probability 1;
  • \(y_{0} \oplus y_{1} = x_{1} \oplus x_{2}\) holds with probability 3/4.
  • The larger the bias, the better the approximation; after propagating along multiple rounds the subkey can be recovered.
  • The DES S-box design means there are no good linear approximations to any one output bit, but linear combinations of output bits can still be approximated by linear combinations of input bits; in practice it requires a huge amount of plaintext and is not very practical.

docs.title: 3.1 Why modes are needed
docs.text:
• A block is only 64/128 bit, while the message is far larger than one block.
  • A new key for each block = as impractical as a one-time pad (key distribution).
  • So a fixed key + chaining/counter is used to handle multiple blocks; partial blocks are not considered in this course.

docs.title: 3.2 ECB (Electronic Codebook) ★
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} C_i &= E(P_i, K) \\ P_i &= D(C_i, K) \end{aligned} \]
  • Same plaintext block → same ciphertext block.
  • Equivalent to "a different codebook for each key".

Problem 1: cut-and-paste

Plaintext: Eva. pings Bob. Ted. pings Tom. (64-bit blocks, 8-bit ASCII) - P0=Eva. pin, P1=gs Bob., P2=Ted. pin, P3=gs Tom. - Ciphertext C0 C1 C2 C3; the attacker rearranges it to C0 C3 C2 C1; - Decrypts to: Eva. pin + gs Tom. + Ted. pin + gs Bob. = Eva. pings Tom. Ted. pings Bob.

Problem 2: pattern leakage

  • Encrypt an uncompressed image and the large-scale outline is still visible — because the same plaintext block produces the same ciphertext block.
  • Even without knowing the plaintext, the attacker knows "which blocks are identical".

docs.title: 3.3 CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) ★
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} C_0 &= E(IV \oplus P_0, K) \\ C_i &= E(C_{i-1} \oplus P_i, K) \\ P_0 &= IV \oplus D(C_0, K) \\ P_i &= C_{i-1} \oplus D(C_i, K) \end{aligned} \]
  • The IV is random, but need not be secret; its role is to turn the same P0 into a different C0.
  • Same plaintext block → different ciphertext blocks (because the chaining value differs).
  • Error propagation is limited: if C1 is garbled, P1 becomes garbled and the corresponding bits of P2 are affected, but P3 onward is normal.
  • Cut-and-paste is still possible (rearranging whole blocks).
  • Malleable: flipping some bit of \(C_{i-1}\) → the same bit of \(P_i\) flips, and \(P_{i-1}\) becomes garbled. If the attacker knows the structure of \(P_i\) (e.g., an amount), a targeted modification is possible → this again shows that encryption does not provide integrity.

Exam point: does the CBC IV need to be secret? — No; does it need to be random/unpredictable? — Yes.

docs.title: 3.4 CTR (Counter) ★
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} C_i &= P_i \oplus E(IV + i, K) \\ P_i &= C_i \oplus E(IV + i, K) \end{aligned} \]
  • Uses the block cipher like a stream cipher; supports random access (you can jump directly to block i).
  • Can be parallelized and precomputed.
  • ⚠ The IV/nonce must never be reused: if the same E(IV) encrypts two messages, then \(C_{1}\oplus C_{2} = P_{1}\oplus P_{2}\), equivalent to a two-time pad.

docs.title: 3.5 Comparing the three modes (memorize this table)
docs.text: Dimension ECB CBC CTR Same plaintext block Same ciphertext Different ciphertext Different ciphertext Parallel encryption Yes No (chained) Yes Random access Yes No Yes Error propagation This block only This block + part of the next This block only Needs an IV No Yes (random) Yes (unique, must not be reused) Main problem Pattern leakage, cut-and-paste Malleable, cut-and-paste nonce reuse disaster Typical use Not recommended File/message encryption Disk/network/random access

docs.title: 3.6 Integrity: MAC ★★
docs.text:
Why a MAC is needed

  • Encryption only prevents "reading", not "modification": a one-time pad can be flipped, ECB can be rearranged, CBC can be bit-flipped.
  • Integrity = detect unauthorized writing.

MAC = CBC residue

\[ \begin{aligned} C_0 &= E(IV \oplus P_0, K) \\ C_1 &= E(C_0 \oplus P_1, K) \\ &\vdots \\ C_{N-1} &= E(C_{N-2} \oplus P_{N-1}, K) = \mathrm{MAC} \end{aligned} \]
  • Send \((IV, P_0\\dots P_{N-1}, MAC)\); the receiver recomputes with the same K and compares the MAC.
  • Why it detects tampering: changing any P_i propagates along the chain to the final MAC; without K a new MAC cannot be forged.

Why encryption and MAC must use different keys

  • If the same key is used, sending the last ciphertext block (the MAC) again cannot add any security;
  • Different keys (even related ones) work, but the cost is about 2× encryption; optimization can bring it down to about 1.5×;
  • AE (authenticated encryption) is the research direction for "providing C + I in one operation".

MAC vs digital signature: in a MAC both parties share the key, so Bob can forge it too → no non-repudiation; a signature uses the private key, and only the signer can produce it → non-repudiation (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 4. Quantum computers and symmetric ciphers
docs.text:
• A qubit can be in a superposition of 0/1; N qubits have \(2^N\) amplitudes.
  • Grover's algorithm: gives a square-root speedup for exhaustive search.
  • Classical: n-bit key, work factor about 2ⁿ;
  • Grover: about \(2^{n/2}\).
  • For AES-128: about \(2^{64}\) after Grover → no longer enough; the countermeasure is AES-256 (about \(2^{128}\) after Grover).
  • Conclusion: quantum is not a serious threat to symmetric ciphers, doubling the key length is enough; the real danger is RSA/DH (Shor, Chapter 3).

docs.title: Example 1: one Feistel round (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: L0=0110, R0=1001, K=1111, F(R,K)=R⊕K. Find (L1,R1) after one round and the ciphertext C.

Solution: - \(L_1 = R_0 = 1001\) - \(R_{1} = L_{0} \oplus F(R_{0},K) = 0110 \oplus (1001\oplus 1111) = 0110 \oplus 0110 = 0000\) - \(C = (R_1, L_1) = (0000, 1001)\)

Scoring points: the formulas are written correctly; the final swap of left and right (the easiest thing to miss).

docs.title: Example 2: 2DES meet-in-the-middle (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: double encryption \(C = E(E(P,K_1),K_2)\), with 56-bit keys. Explain how MITM reduces \(2^{112}\) to about \(2^{57}\).

Solution: 1. For all \(2^{56}\) values of K1, compute \(X = E(P,K_1)\) and store it in a table (sorted/hashed by X). 2. For all \(2^{56}\) values of K2, compute \(Y = D(C,K_2)\). 3. Find the match where \(X = Y\) → candidate (K1,K2), then verify with a second plaintext/ciphertext pair. 4. Time ≈ \(2^{56}\) + \(2^{56}\) = \(2^{57}\), space ≈ \(2^{56}\).

Conclusion: double encryption does not have 112-bit strength; 3DES uses EDE to avoid this direct decomposition.

docs.title: Example 3: ECB cut-and-paste (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: the plaintext consists of 4 64-bit blocks: Eva. pin | gs Bob. | Ted. pin | gs Tom., and the ciphertext is C0 C1 C2 C3. How do you make the decrypted result become Eva. pings Tom. Ted. pings Bob.?

Solution: send C0 C3 C2 C1. - Decryption: P0=Eva. pin, P3=gs Tom., P2=Ted. pin, P1=gs Bob. - Concatenated: Eva. pings Tom. Ted. pings Bob.

Scoring point: state that each ECB block is independent, so the blocks can be rearranged arbitrarily.

docs.title: Example 4: CBC bit flipping (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: in CBC encryption, the attacker flips the 3rd bit of C1. Which plaintext blocks are affected after decryption? Can the attacker modify P2 in a targeted way?

Solution: - P1 is computed from D(C1) → if C1 changes, the whole of P1 becomes garbled (unpredictable); - P2 = C1 ⊕ D(C2) → flipping the 3rd bit of C1 makes the 3rd bit of P2 flip exactly; - So the attacker cannot control P1, but can flip any bit of P2 in a targeted way (as long as the structure of P2 is known). - Conclusion: CBC encryption does not provide integrity; a MAC/AE must be added.

docs.title: Example 5: Grover (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: how much security strength does AES-128 have left under quantum computing? What should be done?

Solution: - Grover reduces exhaustive search from \(2^{128}\) to about \(2^{64}\); - \(2^{64}\) is no longer enough for modern computing power → switch to AES-256, about \(2^{128}\) after Grover; - The only cost is being "a little slower", which is acceptable.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes (where marks are most easily lost)
docs.text: Mistake Correct Two-key 3DES strength = 168 bit Two keys give about 112 bit; only three keys give about 168 "\(2^{57}\) is the strength of 3DES" \(2^{57}\) is the MITM cost for double encryption, 2DES; 3DES EDE is about 112 bit Feistel decryption requires F to be invertible It does not; Feistel is invertible for any F, but security depends on F AES is a Feistel cipher It is not; AES is an SPN (substitution-permutation network) 3DES uses EDE to be "harder to crack" The primary purpose is backward compatibility with single-key DES; it also avoids the 2DES MITM The CBC IV must be secret The IV need not be secret, but it must be random/unpredictable The CTR nonce may be repeated Absolutely not; reuse is equivalent to a two-time pad Encryption also guarantees integrity It does not; a MAC/signature/AE is required A MAC provides non-repudiation It does not; both parties share the key, so Bob can forge it too Grover breaks AES It only halves the strength; AES-256 restores 128-bit security RC5 is an upgrade of RC4 RC5 is a block cipher, unrelated to RC4

docs.title: 7. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. What is the essential difference between stream ciphers and block ciphers? Give two algorithms for each.
  2. How does A5/1's majority clocking work? How is the output bit computed?
  3. What do RC4's KSA and PRGA each do? Why must the first 256 bytes be discarded?
  4. Write the Feistel encryption and decryption formulas; why is it that "any F can decrypt, but not any F is secure"?
  5. What are DES's block, key, rounds, subkey length, and S-box specification? Where does the security come from?
  6. Why does 3DES use EDE? Why not \(E(E(P,K_1),K_2)\)?
  7. What are the four AES round operations and what does each do? Why is it said not to be a Feistel cipher?
  8. What are ECB's two fatal problems? How does CBC solve them? What problems remain in CBC?
  9. Why must the CTR nonce never be reused? Give the quantity the attacker can compute directly.
  10. Why can a MAC detect tampering? Why must encryption and MAC use different keys?
  11. What does Grover mean for AES-128/256 respectively?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. Stream ciphers generate a keystream bit/byte at a time (A5/1, RC4); block ciphers iterate a round function over fixed-sized blocks (DES, AES).
  2. \(m = \mathrm{maj}(x_8,y_{10},z_{10})\); only registers whose clocking bit equals m step; output \(x_{18}\oplus y_{21}\oplus z_{22}\).
  3. The KSA uses the key to scramble the 256-byte permutation table; the PRGA swaps and outputs 1 byte per step; the first 256 bytes have a statistical bias, and keeping them can be exploited.
  4. \(L_{i+1}=R_i\), \(R_{i+1}=L_i\oplus F(R_i,K_i)\), \(C=(R_{n+1},L_{n+1})\); decryption runs in reverse with the subkeys in reverse order. Every round is invertible, so F need not be invertible; but with \(F=0\) only a swap remains, with no confusion at all.
  5. 64/56/16/48/8 S-boxes (6→4). The security comes mainly from the non-linearity of the S-boxes.
  6. EDE degrades to DES when K1=K2 (backward compatible); \(E(E(P,K_1),K_2)\) is reduced by MITM from \(2^{112}\) to about \(2^{57}\).
  7. ByteSub (non-linearity), ShiftRow (row diffusion), MixColumn (column diffusion), AddRoundKey (key injection). AES processes the whole 128-bit state each round, not just half of it.
  8. The same plaintext block produces the same ciphertext → pattern leakage; blocks can be rearranged → cut-and-paste. CBC uses chaining and a random IV to solve "same block"; but whole-block rearrangement and bit flipping are still possible.
  9. \(C_{1}\oplus C_{2} = P_{1}\oplus P_{2}\); the same E(IV) is used twice, so the XOR of the two ciphertexts is the XOR of the two plaintexts.
  10. Changing any plaintext block propagates along the CBC chain to the final MAC; without K it cannot be forged. Under the same key the MAC and the ciphertext can "borrow" from each other, and sending it twice adds no security; different keys separate the purposes.
  11. AES-128 → about \(2^{64}\) (not enough); AES-256 → about \(2^{128}\) (enough); the cost is being a little slower.

docs.title: 8. Pre-exam quick-reference card
docs.text: Item Value / key point A5/1 19/22/23 bit; majority clocking; output \(x_{18}\oplus y_{21}\oplus z_{22}\) RC4 256-byte permutation; discard the first 256 bytes; RC5 is a block cipher Feistel \(L'=R, R'=L\oplus F(R,K)\); \(C=(R,L)\); F need not be invertible DES 64/56/16/48; 8 S-boxes (6→4); security relies on the S-boxes DES cracking 1998 EFF < $250k, < 3 days; 1999 22h15m 3DES EDE, two keys 112 bit; three keys 168 bit 2DES MITM \(2^{112}\) → about \(2^{57}\) AES 128-bit block; 128/192/256-bit key; 10/12/14 rounds; ByteSub/ShiftRow/MixColumn/AddRoundKey TEA 64/128; 32 rounds; delta=0x9e3779b9; equivalent keys \(2^{128}\)→\(2^{126}\) ECB same plaintext block, same ciphertext; cut-paste; pattern leakage CBC \(C_i=E(C_{i-1}\oplus P_i)\); IV random and not secret; bit flipping possible CTR \(C_i=P_i\oplus E(IV+i)\); nonce must not be reused; random access MAC CBC residue; different keys for encryption/MAC; about 1.5–2× overhead Grover \(2^{n/2}\); AES-256 restores 128-bit security

docs.title: Chapter 3 · Public Key Cryptography · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w3/public-key-cryptography.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 80 minutes + worked examples 40 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.4

Weight of this chapter: RSA computation, DH key exchange, signatures/certificates, and the hash birthday bound are high-frequency sources of computation and short-answer questions; Shor's algorithm is often examined in comparison with Grover from Chapter 2.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. Public key cryptography uses a trapdoor one-way function to solve "how do we distribute keys securely": encrypt with the public key, decrypt with the private key; for signatures it is the other way round.
  2. RSA's security = integer factorization; DH's security = discrete log; both fear Shor's algorithm, while symmetric ciphers are only affected by Grover.
  3. Public key algorithms are slow and have a message length limit, so real systems are a hybrid of "public key to establish a key + symmetric to encrypt the data"; binding a public key to an identity relies on PKI/certificates, and signing a large message relies on hashing first.

Common question types in this chapter
