Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare RSA computation Given small p, q, e, find d, encrypt, decrypt, sign Be able to do extended Euclid/trial and error; be able to do repeated squaring Protocol analysis Why does DH fear man-in-the-middle? How do you prevent it? Draw the three-party key table Concept discrimination Signature vs MAC; encryption vs signature Grab "is the key shared?" Hash computation Cost of the birthday attack, the value at the d-th step of a hash chain Remember \(2^{N/2}\) and the index PKI What is in a certificate? Why is a CA trusted? Memorize the X.509 fields + the chain of trust

docs.title: 1.1 Trapdoor one-way function
docs.text:
• One-way: easy in the forward direction, extremely hard in the reverse direction.
  • Trapdoor: once you hold a certain secret (the private key), the reverse direction becomes easy.
  • Typical: \(N = p\cdot q\) is easy; factoring p and q out of N is extremely hard. The trapdoor is p and q.

docs.title: 1.2 Two uses (must be distinguished)
docs.text:
Purpose What the sender uses What the receiver uses Provides Encryption (secrecy) Bob's public key Bob's private key Confidentiality Signature (authentication) Alice's private key Alice's public key Integrity + authentication + non-repudiation

Mnemonic: encryption is "locking with the other party's public key", a signature is "stamping with your own private key".

docs.title: 2.1 Key generation ★★
docs.text:
1. Choose two large primes p and q.
  2. \(N = p\cdot q\) (the modulus).
  3. Compute \(\varphi (N) = (p-1)(q-1)\).
  4. Choose e such that \(\gcd(e, \varphi (N)) = 1\) (usually e=65537).
  5. Find d such that \(e\cdot d \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi (N})\) (extended Euclid).
  6. Public key (N, e); private key d (p and q must be kept secret/destroyed).

docs.title: 2.2 Encryption and decryption ★★
docs.text:
Encryption: \(C = M^e \bmod N\); decryption: \(M = C^d \bmod N\).

Correctness intuition: \(C^d = M^{ed} = M^{1+k\varphi (N)} \equiv M \pmod{N}\); when \(\gcd(M,N)=1\) this follows directly from Euler's theorem, and when they are not coprime it can also be proved with CRT (since N is the product of two primes). In practice the probability that M is not coprime to N is negligible.

docs.title: 2.3 Security = factoring N ★★
docs.text:
• If an attacker can factor \(N = p\cdot q\), they can compute \(\varphi (N)\) and then derive d from e.
  • Therefore: factoring the modulus breaks RSA.
  • But "RSA hard ≠ factoring hard" is an unproven equivalence; currently there is no general attack faster than factoring.

docs.title: 2.4 Efficiency: repeated squaring ★
docs.text:
Computing \(M^e\) directly produces astronomically large numbers; you must take the modulus at each step.

Example: compute \(5^{20} \bmod 35\).

\[ \begin{aligned} 5^1 &= 5\\ 5^2 &= 25\\ 5^4 &= 25^2 = 625 \equiv 30 \pmod{35}\\ 5^5 &= 5^4\cdot 5 = 30\cdot 5 = 150 \equiv 10 \pmod{35}\\ 5^{10} &= 10^2 = 100 \equiv 30 \pmod{35}\\ 5^{20} &= 30^2 = 900 \equiv 25 \pmod{35} \end{aligned} \]
  • First write the exponent in binary, then go bit by bit: "square, and multiply by the base when the bit is 1".
  • Intermediate values always stay < N², so nothing blows up.
  • You can precompute a table of the commonly used powers.

docs.title: 2.5 Message length and hybrid encryption ★★
docs.text:
• RSA can only encrypt numbers smaller than N; a 2048-bit modulus = 256 bytes.
  • Real padding (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) takes another 11 bytes → at most about 245 bytes of plaintext.
  • Do not "cut the message into chunks and RSA each one": ciphertext expansion, slow, plus padding/mode problems.
  • Hybrid cryptosystem:
  • Use RSA to encrypt a random symmetric key (or establish a key);
  • Use a symmetric cipher such as AES to encrypt the actual data.
  • SSL/TLS and OpenPGP both do this.
  • But "how does Bob confirm that the public key really belongs to Alice?" → certificates are needed (§5).

docs.title: 2.6 RSA numbers (for awareness)
docs.text:
• RSA Labs published semiprimes (exactly two prime factors) with 100–617 decimal digits.
  • As of 2018-08, 20 of the 54 have been factored.
  • RSA-100 (330 bit) is the easiest; no one can break RSA-2048 so far.
  • Key collisions: the probability that two independently generated RSA key pairs happen to be identical is extremely low (the slides only give an informal explanation; no need to dig deeper).
  • Conclusion: real deployments use at least 2048-bit and are gradually migrating to 3072/4096.

docs.title: 2.7 Pitfalls of textbook RSA (supplementary, but "why is padding needed" is often examined)
docs.text:
• Deterministic: the same M always gives the same C → dictionary/replay attacks work; randomized padding is needed (OAEP).
  • Malleable: \(C_{1}\cdot C_{2} = (M_{1}\cdot M_{2})^e\) → an attacker can construct related plaintexts.
  • Signatures are forgeable: \(S(M_{1})\cdot S(M_{2}) = S(M_{1}\cdot M_{2})\) → an attacker can obtain a signature on \(M_{1}\cdot M_{2}\) without asking for it; hash + padding is needed.
  • Small e / common modulus / low-entropy plaintext: all have classic attacks (not covered in this course).

docs.title: 3.1 Protocol
docs.text:
Public parameters: a large prime p, a generator g.

  1. Alice picks a secret a, computes \(A = g^a \bmod p\), and sends it to Bob.
  2. Bob picks a secret b, computes \(B = g^b \bmod p\), and sends it to Alice.
  3. Alice computes \(K = B^a = g^{ab} \bmod p\).
  4. Bob computes \(K = A^b = g^{ab} \bmod p\).
  5. Both sides obtain the same symmetric key K.

DH is not used for encrypting/signing, only for establishing a key.

docs.title: 3.2 Security = discrete log
docs.text:
• The attacker can see \(g, p, A=g^a, B=g^b\).
  • If they can find a from \(g^a\) (the discrete log problem), they can compute \(K = B^a\).
  • Note: \(A\cdot B = g^{a+b} \neq g^{ab}\) — you cannot get the key by multiplying directly.

docs.title: 3.3 Man-in-the-middle (MiM) attack ★
docs.text:
1. Trudy intercepts Alice's \(g^a\), picks her own t, and sends \(g^t\) to Bob.
  2. Trudy intercepts Bob's \(g^b\) and sends \(g^t\) to Alice.
  3. Alice computes \(K_AT = g^{at}\); Bob computes \(K_BT = g^{bt}\); Trudy can compute both.
  4. After that Trudy talks to Alice with K_AT and to Bob with K_BT, and neither side has any idea.

Root cause: DH itself has no authentication — Alice cannot confirm that \(g^t\) came from Bob. Defense: authenticate DH's public values with certificates/signatures/pre-shared keys (e.g., TLS's signed key exchange, Signal's X3DH, etc.).

docs.title: 3.4 Small example (p=23, g=5, a=6, b=15)
docs.text: \[ \begin{aligned} A &= 5^6 \bmod 23 = 8\\ B &= 5^{15} \bmod 23 = 19\\ \text{Alice: } K &= 19^6 \bmod 23 = 2\\ \text{Bob: } K &= 8^{15} \bmod 23 = 2 \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: 4.1 Mechanism
docs.text:
• Sign: \(S = [M]_{\\text{Alice}} = M^d \bmod N\) ("encrypt" with the private key).
  • Verify: \(M = S^e \bmod N\) ("decrypt" with the public key).
  • Only Alice knows d, so only she can produce S; anyone can verify.

docs.title: 4.2 Why it gives non-repudiation ★
docs.text:
MAC Digital signature Key Both sides share K The signer alone holds the private key Can Bob forge it Yes (he also knows K) No (he does not have d) Can it be proved to a third party No Yes Non-repudiation None Yes

Scenario: Alice orders 100 shares from Bob. - With a MAC: after the stock drops Alice denies it; Bob cannot prove that he did not forge it himself (he also has K). - With a signature: only Alice has the private key; Bob can verify the signature to a judge → Alice cannot repudiate. - Precondition: the private key has not been stolen/leaked.

docs.title: 4.3 Hash-then-sign ★★
docs.text:
• Signing a large message directly: RSA is slow, and the signature length = the message length (impractical).
  • Instead sign h(M): \(S = [h(M)]_{\text{Alice}}\), and send (M, S).
  • Verify: compute h(M) and compare it with \(S^e\).
  • Precondition: the hash must be collision resistant; otherwise an attacker finds M' with \(h(M')=h(M)\) and can replace (M,S) with (M',S).
  • This explains why broken collisions in MD5/SHA-1 directly threaten signature security.

docs.title: 4.4 The "direction" of signature vs encryption (easy to get wrong)
docs.text:
• Encryption: public key encrypts → private key decrypts.
  • Signature: private key "encrypts" → public key "decrypts".
  • Do not treat "encrypting a message with the private key" as "keeping the message secret" — anyone can open it with the public key, it provides no confidentiality.

docs.title: 5.1 The problem
docs.text:
• You receive (M, S) — how do you know that this "Alice's public key" really belongs to Alice?
  • An attacker can forge "Alice's public key" and then sign with their own private key.
  • Solution: a trusted third party, the CA, vouches for "identity + public key".

docs.title: 5.2 Digital certificate
docs.text:
• Contents: user name, public key, validity period, issuer, etc.
  • Signed by the CA with the CA's private key.
  • Verify: use the CA's public key to verify the certificate signature → trust the public key in the certificate.
  • Common format: X.509.

Main X.509 fields (being able to list 5 is enough):

 1Version
 2Serial Number
 3Signature Algorithm
 4Issuer Name
 5Validity Period
 6Subject Name
 7Subject Public Key
 8Issuer Unique ID
 9Subject Unique ID
10Extensions
11Digital Signature

docs.title: 5.3 Certificate life cycle
docs.text:
1Key pair generated → Certificate issued → Key pair in use → Certificate expires / private key compromised → Certificate revoked (CRL) → Re-certify / new key pair
  • CRL (Certificate Revocation List): the CA publishes a list of "revoked certificates".
  • Revocation checking is the practical difficulty of PKI (CRLs too large; OCSP privacy/availability problems).

docs.title: 5.4 Why trust a CA?
docs.text:
• Root CA certificates are preinstalled in the OS/browser/application since installation time, and updated with normal system updates.
  • The CA verifies identity by real-world measures (business license, domain control, phone callback), not by cryptography.
  • Trust is transitive: root CA → intermediate CA → site certificate.
  • Risk: a CA is compromised/acts maliciously → it can issue arbitrary certificates (this has happened historically).

docs.title: 5.5 Three trust models
docs.text: Model Structure Example Monopoly A single/very few root CAs Early browser vendor roots Oligarchy A few trusted CAs (most common) The modern TLS ecosystem Anarchy Anyone can be a CA, relying on self-certification/reputation PGP web of trust

docs.title: 6.1 The five properties (must memorize)
docs.text: Property Meaning Attack it resists Compression any length → fixed n-bit — Efficiency easy to compute — One-way (preimage) given y, cannot find x with H(x)=y reversing plaintext/passwords Weak collision (second preimage) given x, cannot find y≠x with H(y)=H(x) tampering with a single message Strong collision cannot find any pair y≠x with H(y)=H(x) forging an arbitrary message

docs.title: 6.2 Birthday problems ★★
docs.text:
• Pre-birthday problem (weak collision): finding someone with the same birthday as me takes 253 people.
  • Birthday problem (strong collision): any two people sharing a birthday needs only 23 people.
  • Generalization: for an N-bit hash, about \(2^{N/2}\) tries are enough to find a collision.
  • Corollaries:
  • An N-bit hash has only N/2 bits of security strength;
  • 128-bit (MD5) → \(2^{64}\); 160-bit (SHA-1) → \(2^{80}\);
  • whereas an N-bit symmetric key has about N bits of strength.

docs.title: 6.3 Common algorithms
docs.text:
Algorithm Output Status MD5 128 bit collisions easy to construct, broken SHA-1 160 bit crackable since 2005, no longer recommended SHA-256/384/512 256/384/512 currently secure SHA-3 224/256/384/512 different structure (sponge), secure
  • Structure: Merkle–Damgård: a fixed compression function + block-by-block iteration, where the previous block's output takes part in the next block; no key involved, similar to a block cipher.
  • Avalanche effect: MD5("...dog") and MD5("...dog.") give completely different outputs.

docs.title: 6.4 Clever uses of hashing
docs.text:
(1) Password storage (detailed in Chapter 7)

  • Store h(password); an attacker precomputes a dictionary → cracked in seconds.
  • Add a salt: store (s, h(password, s)); the attacker must recompute for every user.

(2) Hash chains / one-time passwords

  • 24 classes, secret t:
  • class 1 gets H²³(t);
  • class d gets \(H^{24-d}(t)\);
  • class 24 gets t.
  • Verify: hash the received value once more; it should equal the previous value.
  • Security: from the current value you cannot derive the next value (that requires inverting); also each value corresponds to exactly one class, so a replay is rejected by the index check.

(3) Anti-spam PoW

  • Require the first N bits of h(M, R, T) to be zero.
  • The sender tries \(2^N\) times on average; the receiver needs only 1 verification.
  • N is adjustable: acceptable for normal email, while the cost for spam rises exponentially.
  • Blockchain PoW has the same origin.

docs.title: 6.5 Quantum computing: Shor ★★
docs.text:
• Shor's algorithm (1994) can factor large integers and solve discrete logs in polynomial time.
  • For a 2048-bit modulus:
  • the number field sieve (best classic) ≈ 125-bit symmetric key strength;
  • Shor ≈ 30-bit symmetric key strength.
  • Conclusion: RSA, DH, and DSA/ECDSA all fail; symmetric ciphers with long keys survive.
  • Countermeasure: post-quantum cryptography (e.g., NTRU, lattice-based cryptography) — the slides only name NTRU.

docs.title: Example 1: RSA full flow (12 points)
docs.text:
Question: p=11, q=3, e=3, M=8. Find N, φ(N), d, the ciphertext C, and verify the decryption.

Solution: - \(N = 11\times 3 = 33\) - \(\varphi (N) = 10\times 2 = 20\) - \(e=3\), \(3d \equiv 1 \pmod{20}\) → \(d=7\) (3×7=21≡1) - \(C = 8^{3} \bmod 33 = 512 \bmod 33 = 17\) - Verify: \(17^{7} \bmod 33\) - \(17^{2} = 289 \equiv 25\) - \(17^{4} = 25^{2} = 625 \equiv 31\) - \(17^{7} = 17^{4}\cdot 17^{2}\cdot 17 = 31\cdot 25\cdot 17 \equiv 16\cdot 17 = 272 \equiv 8\) ✓

Marking points: φ computed correctly; d satisfies \(ed\equiv 1\); decryption uses repeated squaring rather than brute force.

docs.title: Example 2: DH key exchange (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: p=23, g=5, Alice's a=6, Bob's b=15. Find A, B, and the shared key K.

Solution: - \(A = 5^{6} \bmod 23 = 8\) - \(B = 5^{15} \bmod 23 = 19\) - Alice: \(K = B^a = 19^{6} \bmod 23 = 2\) - Bob: \(K = A^b = 8^{15} \bmod 23 = 2\)

Marking points: both sides compute the same K; state that security depends on the discrete log.

docs.title: Example 3: DH man-in-the-middle (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: describe how Trudy, without breaking the discrete log, makes Alice and Bob each believe they are communicating with the other.

Solution: 1. Trudy picks t, intercepts \(g^a\), and sends \(g^t\) to Bob; 2. intercepts \(g^b\) and sends \(g^t\) to Alice; 3. Alice gets \(g^{at}\), Bob gets \(g^{bt}\), and Trudy can compute both; 4. Trudy decrypts/forwards with the two keys respectively, and neither side notices.

Defense: authenticate DH's exchanged values (certificates/signatures/pre-shared keys).

docs.title: Example 4: Birthday attack (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: a system uses a 128-bit hash for integrity checking. How many tries does an attacker need to forge a second preimage? How many to find an arbitrary collision?

Solution: - Second preimage (given x, find y): about \(2^{128}\); - Arbitrary collision (birthday): about \(2^{64}\); - So a 128-bit hash has only 64 bits of "collision resistance", which is no longer enough; at least 256-bit should be used.

docs.title: Example 5: Hash chain (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: 24 classes, secret t, class 1 sends H²³(t). What should class 5 send? How does the verifier verify it?

Solution: - Class d sends \(H^{24-d}(t)\); d=5 → H¹⁹(t). - Verify: hash the previous value once more; it should equal the value received in class 4 (\(H(H^{19})=H^{20}\)). - An attacker holding H¹⁹(t) cannot derive H¹⁸(t) (that requires inverting the hash), so they cannot forge the next value in advance.

docs.title: Example 6: Why RSA needs padding (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: what is the problem with using \(C=M^e\) directly in textbook RSA?

Solution: - Deterministic: the same M produces the same C, so dictionary/replay attacks work; - Malleable: \(C_{1}\cdot C_{2} = (M_{1}M2)^e\); - Signatures are forgeable: \(S(M_{1})\cdot S(M_{2}) = S(M_{1}M2)\). - Fix: use randomized padding such as OAEP for encryption; use hash + PSS/PKCS#1 v1.5 for signatures.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes (where marks are most easily lost)
docs.text: Mistake Correct The RSA private key is (N,d) and the public key is (N,e) Correct; but p, q, and φ(N) must be kept secret/destroyed A signature = encrypting with the private key, so it also keeps things secret Wrong; anyone can open it with the public key, it provides no confidentiality Sign the message directly, no hash needed Not feasible for large messages; textbook RSA signatures are also malleable; you must hash-then-sign A MAC gives non-repudiation It does not; both sides share the key DH can encrypt data DH only establishes a key, it does not encrypt/sign \(g^a\cdot g^b\) in DH is the shared key Wrong; it is \(g^{a+b}\), the shared key is \(g^{ab}\) A certificate contains only the public key It also has the identity, validity period, issuer, signature, etc. A root CA is trusted because of cryptography It is because of preinstallation + real-world identity verification; cryptography only guarantees signature integrity An N-bit hash = N-bit security Collision resistance is only N/2 bit Shor breaks AES Shor breaks RSA/DH; AES only fears Grover (strength halved) Multiplying two large primes is hard to factor, so RSA must be secure There is currently no general attack faster than factoring, but "RSA hard ⇔ factoring hard" is unproven

docs.title: 9. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. What do "one-way" and "trapdoor" each refer to in a trapdoor one-way function? Give an example.
  2. Write out RSA key generation, encryption, and decryption; why does factoring N break RSA?
  3. Why does RSA need "mod at each step + repeated squaring"? How many bytes can a 2048-bit RSA encrypt at most?
  4. What is hybrid encryption? Why do real systems not encrypt data directly with RSA?
  5. Write out the DH protocol flow; why can an attacker who sees \(g^a\) and \(g^b\) not obtain \(g^{ab}\) directly?
  6. How does the DH man-in-the-middle attack happen? How do you defend against it?
  7. Why do digital signatures give non-repudiation while a MAC does not?
  8. Why must you hash before signing? What happens if the hash is collidable?
  9. Which fields does a certificate contain? How is the CA's signature verified? Why is a root CA trusted?
  10. What are the five properties of a hash? Why is the birthday attack \(2^{N/2}\)?
  11. How does a hash chain implement one-time passwords? Why can an attacker not compute the next value in advance?
  12. What does Shor's algorithm mean for RSA/DH? Why are symmetric ciphers not affected the same way?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. Easy to compute forward, hard to compute in reverse; once you have the trapdoor (private key), the reverse becomes easy. Example: N=pq is easy to compute, factoring N is hard, and p and q are the trapdoor.
  2. Choose \(p,q\); \(N=pq\); \(\varphi=(p-1)(q-1)\); choose \(e\) coprime to \(\varphi\); find \(d\) with \(ed\equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi}\); public key \((N,e)\), private key \(d\). Encrypt \(C=M^e\), decrypt \(M=C^d\). Factor \(N\) to get \(p,q\) → compute \(\varphi\) → use \(e\) to find \(d\).
  3. Computing \(M^e\) directly produces huge integers; taking the modulus at each step keeps values \(<N^2\), and repeated squaring cuts the number of multiplications to \(O(\log e)\). 2048-bit → 256 bytes, about 245 bytes after padding.
  4. The public key only encrypts/wraps one symmetric key, and the data is encrypted with AES. RSA is slow, limited in message length, and expands the ciphertext; it is unsuitable for transmitting large amounts of data.
  5. Alice sends \(g^a\), Bob sends \(g^b\); both sides compute \(g^{ab}\). The attacker only has \(g^a\) and \(g^b\), whose product is \(g^{a+b}\); obtaining \(g^{ab}\) requires solving CDH/discrete log.
  6. Trudy establishes a key with each side using \(g^t\), holds both keys, and forwards traffic. Defense: authenticated DH (certificates/signatures/pre-shared keys).
  7. Only Alice has the signing private key, Bob cannot forge it, and it can be verified to a third party; for a MAC both sides have K, so Bob can generate it too.
  8. Signing a large message directly is slow and the signature is too long; hashing compresses the message into a fixed-length fingerprint. If the hash is collidable, an attacker can replace (M,S) with (M',S) and verification still passes.
  9. Version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity period, subject, subject public key, extensions, signature, etc. Verify the signature with the CA's public key. Root CAs are preinstalled in the system/browser, and their identity rests on real-world verification.
  10. Compression, efficiency, one-way, weak collision, strong collision. Birthday paradox: comparing all pairs, about \(\sqrt{2^N}=2^{N/2}\) tries give an expected collision.
  11. Class d gets \(H^{24-d}(t)\); the verifier hashes the current value once more and compares it with the previous one. Going from \(H^k(t)\) to \(H^{k-1}(t)\) requires inverting the hash.
  12. Shor can factor/solve discrete logs in polynomial time → RSA, DH, and ECDSA fail; symmetric ciphers only get a square-root speedup from Grover, so doubling the key is enough.

docs.title: 10. Pre-exam quick-reference card
docs.text: Item Content Trapdoor one-way easy forward, hard reverse, easy with the trapdoor RSA key N=pq; φ=(p−1)(q−1); ed≡1 mod φ; public key (N,e), private key d RSA encryption/decryption \(C=M^e \bmod N\); \(M=C^d \bmod N\) RSA security factoring N RSA length 2048-bit ≈ 245 bytes of plaintext Repeated squaring square + multiply on a 1; mod at each step Hybrid encryption RSA wraps the symmetric key + AES encrypts the data DH public \(g,p\); private \(a,b\); exchange \(g^a,g^b\); \(K=g^{ab}\) DH security discrete log; fears MiM; needs authentication Signature private key signs, public key verifies; non-repudiation; hash first Signature vs MAC a signature is asymmetric and gives non-repudiation; a MAC is symmetric and does not Certificate identity+public key+validity period+CA signature; X.509 Chain of trust root CA preinstalled → intermediate CA → site Five hash properties compression, efficiency, one-way, weak collision, strong collision Birthday bound N-bit → \(2^{N/2}\); 23 people / 253 people Hash chain class d gets \(H^{24-d}(t)\); verify by hashing once more PoW first N bits are zero; sender \(2^N\), receiver 1 Shor RSA/DH fail; symmetric only fears Grover

docs.title: Chapter 4 · Malware & Reverse Engineering · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w4/malware.pdf, w4/reverse-engineering.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 90 minutes + worked examples 30 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.5, §2.6

Weight of this chapter: concept discrimination (worm/virus/trojan/backdoor), pros and cons of detection methods, the RE pipeline and disassembly, and the software crack steps — all regulars in short-answer questions.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. Malware has only one goal: get the attacker's code running on your machine; classification is about "how it propagates, how it disguises itself, how it persists".
  2. Detection is an arms race: static signatures are fast but fear mutation, dynamic behavior can catch the unknown but fears sandbox evasion, clustering speeds up analysis but is not detection.
  3. Reverse engineering is "reading a program" when there is no source code: compilation is a many-to-one one-way mapping; disassembly splits into linear/recursive, and decompilation is "disassembly → variable/type recovery → control-flow recovery → code generation".

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Classification What is the difference between worm and virus? trojan and backdoor? Memorize on the three axes "does it self-replicate / does it disguise itself / does it bypass authentication" Case analysis Propagation mechanism and lessons of Morris/Slammer Memorize the numbers + the three intrusion routes Detection design Given a scenario, choose signature/behavior/clustering and state the limitations Memorize the pros-and-cons table RE concepts Linear vs recursive disassembly; disassembler vs decompiler Be able to draw the pipeline Crack workflow How to bypass a serial number with disassembly + patch Memorize the 5 steps + little-endian

docs.title: 1.1 Types (no strict standard definition; memorize by feature) ★
docs.text:
Type Core feature Propagation Typical behavior Worm Self-replicating, active propagation Exploits vulnerabilities to scan/infect automatically Exhausts bandwidth/resources, violates availability Virus Modifies the host program/boot sector, passive propagation Attaches to executables, runs with the program Infects more files Trojan horse Disguised as legitimate software, contains unexpected functionality The user installs it voluntarily Does not duplicate itself; can usually be controlled remotely Backdoor A covert entry point that bypasses normal authentication Implantation/supply chain Remote/local unauthorized access Ransomware Encrypts data and demands a ransom Phishing/vulnerabilities Violates availability (+ confidentiality)

One-line distinction: - Can propagate on its own → worm; propagates by attaching to files → virus; tricks you into installing it → trojan; leaves a hidden door → backdoor.

docs.title: 1.2 Worm case studies ★★
docs.text:
Morris Worm (1988-11-03)

  • Author: Robert Morris, a 23-year-old doctoral student at Cornell; the program was about 99 lines.
  • Three intrusion routes:
  • buffer overflow in fingerd;
  • buffer overflow in sendmail;
  • Guessing weak passwords (a list of common passwords).
  • The flaws were well-known for a long time, but the patches were not widely deployed.
  • Damage: exponential-rate growth + repeated infection → machines lose response → violation of Availability.
  • Significance: the Internet of the time was said to be "designed to survive nuclear war", yet a single graduate student brought it down → shock to the security community, more security awareness.

SQL Slammer (2003)

  • A single 376-byte UDP packet is enough to propagate; 75,000 systems infected in 10 minutes.
  • Exploits a bug in database software; the patch had been released 6 months earlier.
  • At its peak, infections doubled every 8.5 seconds.
  • Why it "burned out" later: it spread too fast and exhausted the available bandwidth, which in turn limited further spread.

Exam point: the danger of a worm is not damage to a single machine but exponential propagation; a patch existing ≠ the patch being applied.

docs.title: 1.3 Viruses and PE files ★
docs.text:
Windows executable format: PE (Portable Executable)

Virus infection steps (memorize these three):

11. Modify the PE header (e.g., the entry point AddressOfEntryPoint)
22. Attach a malicious code section (new section)
33. Redirect the execution flow to the malicious section
  • Variants: append to the end of the file, insert into code caves, infect the import table, etc. (the slides only cover the basic three steps).
  • Where viruses live:
  • Boot sector: takes control before anything else;
  • Applications;
  • Library routines;
  • Compilers, debuggers, virus checker: particularly nasty (infecting the toolchain).

docs.title: 1.4 Trojan horses, backdoors, and the supply chain ★
docs.text:
Mac trojan freeMusic.mp3

  • The icon/extension looks like mp3, but it is actually an application (not data).
  • Double click: iTunes opens (expected) + "Wild Laugh"/message box (not expected).
  • Damage: it could have done anything the user could do (delete files, download files, launch apps).
  • Lesson: extensions/icons can be forged; do not double-click "media files" of unknown origin.

Android App repackaging

1Download a popular app → decompile → insert malicious code → repack → distribute
  • Lesson: do not download APKs from unofficial stores.

Backdoor

  • Listens on some port (e.g., ABC), bypasses local password authentication, and provides remote access.
  • Difference from a trojan: a trojan emphasizes "disguise", a backdoor emphasizes "an entry point that bypasses authentication"; real malware often has both.

Reflections on Trusting Trust (Ken Thompson, 1984 Turing Award Lecture)

  • Question: to what extent should one trust a statement that a program is free of Trojan horses?
  • A malicious compiler can implant a backdoor into a program at compile time, while the source code looks completely clean.
  • Real-world case: XcodeGhost (2015) — developers used Xcode from unofficial channels, and the compiled apps carried a backdoor.
  • Conclusion: a root of trust problem; auditing the source code alone is not enough to fully trust a binary.

docs.title: 1.5 Ransomware
docs.text:
• Uses lightweight symmetric key crypto (TEA, Twofish, Blowfish, etc.) to encrypt the victim's data.
  • Detection idea: pattern matching delta — encryption changes file contents in large chunks, producing a recognizable "difference pattern".

docs.title: 1.6 Detection methods ★★
docs.text:
Method Approach Advantages Disadvantages Static signature Search files for a characteristic bit string/wildcards/hash. E.g., W32/Beast's 83EB 0274 EB0E 740A 81EB 0301 0000 Effective on "ordinary" malware; minimal burden for users/administrators; the most popular and the easiest The signature file is large (10s of thousands) → scanning is slow; must be kept up to date; cannot detect if no signature is on hand; advanced malware can evade it Dynamic behavior Monitor for anything "unusual": unusual file access, system misbehavior, unexpected network activity Can find new malware with no signature Must first define "normal", and normal changes over time; accuracy; attackers can "attack slowly" to look normal; usually combined with signatures Malware clustering Compare against known families/samples (VirusTotal, etc.) using similarity/clustering/embedding Speeds up analysis of a large number of unknown samples; reveals the same author/same toolkit Not a detection method itself; depends on the quality of the sample database; can only "classify", not decide on its own

Behavior analysis examples

  • Android: log the system call sequences, e.g. fread("passwordFile") → sendmsg(...), which reflects the suspicious behavior of "reading a password file and then sending it out".
  • Difficulty: the content being sent out with sendmsg is not visible → static analysis/instrumentation is needed.
  • In-browser mining: a large amount of hash computation in WebAssembly → pinpoint "mining" operations during runtime.

Practical execution environment

  • To observe behavior, the execution of suspicious software must be isolated: virtual machine, sandbox, hardware support.
  • Malware can perform sandbox evasion: check whether it is in a virtual environment (e.g., the "Red Pill" trick: check the IDT/time difference/hardware fingerprint), and sleep/not trigger once a sandbox is detected.

docs.title: 1.7 The arms race: encryption and metamorphism ★
docs.text:
Encrypted malware

  • Different key → different "random" bits → no common signature across copies.
  • Detection:
  • Scan for the decryptor code (the decryptor itself still has a signature);
  • Dump the decrypted code during runtime (it always has to decrypt itself before executing).

Metamorphic malware

  • Mutates itself before infecting a new system:
  • Disassemble itself;
  • Insert random variations (permute the code, insert dead code, equivalent substitution);
  • Assemble the resulting code.
  • Result: same functionality, different byte signature → signature detection fails.
  • Detection: dynamic behavior, semantic normalization, similarity analysis (back to "clustering").

Trend: encrypted, polymorphic, metamorphic malware, obfuscation/diversification; malware has become an "ecosystem", and development is moving toward a "software engineering practice".

docs.title: 2.1 Forward and reverse engineering
docs.text:
• Forward: requirement analysis → design → implementation → testing → delivery.
  • Reverse: take a finished product apart, analyze its workings in detail, and gradually recover its more "abstract" and high-level representation and intention.
  • Its place in security:
  • Software RE: the basis of almost all software security missions (neither attacker nor defender has the source code);
  • Protocol RE: intercept the traffic → recover the package structure (Header/Length/Checksum/Command/Data);
  • Algorithm/model RE: magic number, statistically analyze a large number of pairs of queries, DNN reverse engineering;
  • Hardware RE.

Why it is needed: - Attack: find vulnerabilities, crack licensing, analyze malware; - Defense: audit third-party libraries, check the supply chain, fix vulnerabilities; - Re-engineering: code reuse/migration (e.g., migrate a Windows game to ARM).

docs.title: 2.2 Toolchain and terminology ★
docs.text:
1Source code --compiler--> Assembly --assembler--> Executable
2Executable --disassembler--> Assembly
3Executable --decompiler--> Source code (a decompiler contains a disassembler)
Term Role Disassembler Executable file → CPU assembly instructions Decompiler Executable file → source-code-level representation IDA Pro / JEB3 / Hopper Commercial tools (thousands of US dollars) Ghidra NSA's open-source decompiler/reverse engineering framework

Difficulty gap: Java bytecode retains a lot of type/structural information, so decompiling it is much easier than C/C++; after optimization, inlining, and register allocation, C/C++ loses the most information and is the hardest class in reverse engineering.

docs.title: 2.3 Compilation is a "one-way function" ★
docs.text:
Several different source codes can compile to the same piece of machine code:

1if (x != 0) x = 0;
2x = 0;
3if (x==1) ... else if (x==2) ... else x=0;

All of them may generate the same machine code → impossible to uniquely recover the "original source code".

  • But for comprehension/reuse, any semantically equivalent version is acceptable.
  • This explains why decompiler output "looks like C, but is not necessarily the C the original author wrote".

docs.title: 2.4 Disassembly: linear vs recursive ★★
docs.text:
Linear disassembling

  • Starts from the first byte of the code section and decodes instruction by instruction until the end.
  • Problem: the compiler embeds data in the code section (jump tables, constants, alignment padding). 
    1Actual instructions: inst1; jmp data; inst3; inst4 ...
2Linear disassembling: data is also decoded as instructions → everything after it is misaligned
  • This is legit: the compiler can embed data bytes into the code section.

Recursive disassembling

  • Starts from the entry point and follows the control transfers (jmp/call/ret), disassembling only reachable code.
  • Handles "data embedded in code" correctly: jmp jumps over the data, and recursive disassembly does not follow into it.
  • The CPU executes along the control flow anyway → recursive disassembly is closer to the real semantics.

Exam point: given a byte sequence where "jmp skips over data", ask what linear/recursive disassembly each sees.

docs.title: 2.5 The modern C/C++ decompilation pipeline ★★
docs.text:
1Executable
2 → Disassembly (disassembling)
3 → Variable/Type Recovery (variable and type recovery)
4 → Control-Flow Recovery (control-flow recovery)
5 → Optimization (optimization)
6 → Code Generation (code generation)
7 → Decompiler Output

Variable recovery

  • Divide the "whole block of memory" into variables: bytes that are always used together → one variable.
  • Example: byte1 byte2 always appear together → potentially a variable of two bytes.

Type recovery = type inference

1b = *a;              // a must be a pointer
2printf("%d\n", a);   // a is an integer
3fopen(a, "r");       // a is a string (file name)
  • Variables of different types can have the same length, so the type must be constrained by the way it is used; in essence it is a "deductive proof".

Control-flow recovery

  • Assembly → CFG (control-flow graph); this is the prerequisite to recover if/while/for.
  • Example: identify the back edges of loops and the merge points of branches.

Code generation

  • Pattern matching + concretize code templates: e.g., "this structure should be a for loop".

docs.title: 2.6 Practical defects of decompilation ⚠
docs.text:
Commercial decompilers still make mistakes in variable/type recovery:

Defect Original program Decompiler output Consequence Unreachable loop for (i=6; i<-12; i-=6) never executes Recovered as reachable/iterated many times Semantics changed Shift/truncation (uint8_t)a >> (uint8_t)6 Recovered incorrectly The value of a differs Integer width int32_t a = 0xaaaaffff Recovered as int16_t The result of a+4 differs

Conclusion: decompiler output cannot be trusted directly; manual review/dynamic verification is needed.

docs.title: 2.7 Case study: serial number crack (software crack) ★★
docs.text:
Goal: the program asks for a serial, the correct value is unknown, and only the exe is available.

Steps

  1. Locate the comparison: disassemble, find the cmp on the input and the hardcoded string → see S123N456 directly.
  2. Use it directly: enter S123N456, it passes.
  3. Go further (patch): do not look for the serial number, change the jump directly:
    • Original logic: cmp ...; jne fail (fail if not equal);
    • Change jne to jmp (unconditionally skip the failure) or nop nop (no check).
  4. Hex editing: find the instruction bytes, change them, and save as serialPatch.exe.
  5. Result: any serial number now works.

Addresses and byte order

  • The target address 0x401034 is stored in memory in little-endian order: 34 10 40 00.
  • In ASCII it displays as 4^P@ (0x34='4', 0x10=^P, 0x40='@').
  • Overflow/jump payloads often need the address written "in reverse order".

Conclusion: on an open system it is impossible to prevent SRE; you can only raise the cost (obfuscation, packing, anti-debugging).

docs.title: 2.8 Anti-reverse-engineering techniques
docs.text:
• Anti-disassembly: embed data with code to interfere with linear disassembly.
  • Code obfuscation: layout/data/control-flow obfuscation (Chapter 5).
  • Encryption / packer: pack the binary and unpack it at runtime; unpacking is another battleground.

docs.title: Example 1: worm growth (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: a worm's infection count doubles every 8.5 seconds; how many doublings are there in theory within 10 minutes? Why does it not actually infect \(2^{70}\) machines in reality?

Solution: - 10 minutes = 600 seconds; 600 / 8.5 ≈ 70.6 doublings. - Theoretically about \(2^{70}\) ≈ 1.18×10²¹ machines, far more than the number of hosts worldwide. - In reality it is limited by the number of susceptible hosts, bandwidth, scanning speed, and the size of the target network; Slammer "burned itself out" exactly because it exhausted the available bandwidth.

docs.title: Example 2: PE infection (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: describe how a virus infects a PE file so that the malicious code runs first when the user runs the original program.

Solution: 1. Add a new section to the PE and write the malicious code into it; 2. Modify the entry point (AddressOfEntryPoint) in the PE header so that it points to the new section; 3. After the malicious code finishes, a common practice is to jump back to the original entry point so the program "looks normal" (avoiding a crash the user would notice). - Result: the user double-clicks the original program → the virus runs first → then the normal logic runs.

docs.title: Example 3: limits of signature detection (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: why does static signature detection produce both false negatives and false positives?

Solution: - False negative: new variants/encrypted/metamorphic malware have no known signature → cannot be detected. - False positive: legitimate software may happen to contain the same byte sequence (especially short signatures/wildcards). - In addition, a large signature file → slow scanning; it must be kept up to date.

docs.title: Example 4: linear vs recursive disassembly (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: the code section is actually inst1; jmp data; inst3; ..., and data is data. What do linear and recursive disassembly each see?

Solution: - Linear: decodes byte by byte starting from inst1, treats data as instructions, and everything after it is misaligned. - Recursive: follows the target of jmp (skipping data) and disassembles only the reachable inst3..., never touching data. - Recursive disassembly therefore suits real binaries better; linear suits scenarios where "code and data are strictly separated".

docs.title: Example 5: patching to bypass the check (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: the program checks the serial number with cmp + jne fail. How do you make any serial number pass with hex editing?

Solution: - Find the jne (x86 short jump 75 xx, near jump 0F 85 xx xx xx xx). - Option A: change it to jmp (EB xx / E9 xx xx xx xx) to unconditionally skip the failure branch; - Option B: change it to nop (90 90) so that the comparison result has no effect; - Save as a new exe. - Note: after changing bytes the file length/checksum may change; some programs have integrity checks.

docs.title: Example 6: decompiler defects (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: for (i=6; i<-12; i-=6) is unreachable in the original program; why might the decompiler output become reachable?

Solution: - The loop condition 6 < -12 is always false, but during type recovery/constant folding the decompiler may infer i as unsigned or get the bit width wrong, so the condition is misjudged; - It may also be that CFG recovery incorrectly merges the unreachable block. - This shows that decompiler output needs manual verification and cannot be used directly as source code.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes (where marks are most easily lost)
docs.text: Mistake Correct Both worm and virus self-replicate A virus attaches to a host and propagates passively; a worm self-replicates independently and propagates actively A trojan self-replicates Usually it does not self-replicate; it relies on disguise to trick you into installing it backdoor = trojan A backdoor emphasizes "an entry point that bypasses authentication"; a trojan emphasizes "disguise"; they can overlap but are not equivalent With a patch you cannot be infected by a worm Patches not widely deployed/not rebooted/isolated intranets all still allow infection (Slammer) Signature detection catches all malware It only catches what "has a signature"; encrypted/metamorphic/new variants are missed Dynamic behavior detection is always more accurate It must define "normal"; it can be bypassed by slow attacks/sandbox evasion clustering = detection Clustering speeds up analysis, it is not a decision; a human/other methods are still needed in the end disassembler = decompiler The former goes to assembly, the latter to source code; a decompiler contains a disassembler Linear disassembly is more "complete" It treats data as code; recursive disassembly is closer to real execution Decompiler output can be recompiled and reused directly It often has type/control-flow errors and needs manual repair Cracking requires knowing the serial number You can patch the jump directly and bypass the check An open system can completely prevent RE Impossible; you can only raise the cost

docs.title: 5. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. What are the differences between worm, virus, trojan, and backdoor? Give one example of each.
  2. What were the three intrusion routes of the Morris Worm? Which CIA principle did it violate?
  3. Why did SQL Slammer spread so fast? Why did it "burn itself out"?
  4. Describe the three infection steps of a PE virus.
  5. What is the "Reflections on Trusting Trust" problem? How does XcodeGhost reflect it?
  6. What are the advantages and disadvantages of static signature detection? How can it be evaded?
  7. Why is dynamic behavior detection hard? How can the success rate be improved?
  8. How do encrypted malware and metamorphic malware each evade detection? How are they detected?
  9. Why does linear disassembly fail? How does recursive disassembly solve it?
  10. What are the steps of the decompilation pipeline? Why is variable/type recovery hard?
  11. How do you bypass a serial number check with disassembly + patch? What role does little-endian play in it?
  12. What are the three classes of anti-reverse-engineering techniques?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. worm actively self-replicates (Morris); virus modifies a host and propagates passively (PE virus); trojan disguises itself as legitimate software (freeMusic.mp3); backdoor is an entry point that bypasses authentication (listens on a port).
  2. fingerd buffer overflow, sendmail buffer overflow, guessing weak passwords; it violated availability (it also stole/propagated).
  3. 376-byte single packet, UDP, no handshake needed, many vulnerable hosts, patch not applied → exponential growth; it limited itself by exhausting the available bandwidth.
  4. Modify the PE header entry point; add a new malicious section; redirect the execution flow (jump back to the original entry point after execution).
  5. Trusting the source ≠ trusting the binary; a malicious compiler can implant a backdoor at compile time. XcodeGhost: apps compiled with unofficial Xcode carried a backdoor while the source looked normal.
  6. Advantages: effective on ordinary malware, minimal burden, fast; disadvantages: large signature file, must be updated, false negatives with no signature, can be evaded by encryption/metamorphism. Evasion: packing/encryption, metamorphism, polymorphism.
  7. "Normal" must be defined, and normal changes; attackers can attack slowly/lie low; a sandbox can be detected. Improvement: multi-dimensional monitoring, long runtimes, anti-sandbox countermeasures, combining with signatures.
  8. Encryption: a different key each time → no common signature; detect the decryptor or dump at runtime. Metamorphism: disassemble → mutate → reassemble; detect via dynamic behavior/semantic similarity.
  9. The compiler embeds data in the code section, and linear disassembly treats the data as instructions; recursive disassembly follows the control flow and skips the data.
  10. Disassembly → variable/type recovery → control-flow recovery → optimization → code generation. Difficulties: type information is lost, different variables have equal length, the type must be inferred from usage; optimization destroys the structure.
  11. Find cmp/jne and change jne to jmp or nop; addresses are written in reverse little-endian order (e.g., 0x401034 → 34 10 40 00).
  12. Anti-disassembly (embedding data), obfuscation (layout/data/control flow), packing/encryption.

docs.title: 6. Pre-exam quick-reference card
docs.text: Item Content worm Self-replicates, active propagation; Morris 1988, 99 lines, fingerd/sendmail/weak passwords Slammer 376 B UDP, 75,000 systems/10 min, doubling every 8.5 s, patch 6 months earlier virus Modifies the host/boot sector; PE: modify the header + attach a section + redirect trojan Disguise; does not self-replicate; can be controlled remotely backdoor Bypasses authentication; listens on a port Supply chain Thompson 1984; XcodeGhost 2015 Ransomware Symmetric encryption; pattern matching delta Detection signature (fast, fears mutation) / behavior (catches the unknown, fears evasion) / clustering (speeds up, not detection) Sandbox evasion Detect the virtual machine (Red Pill) Metamorphism Disassemble → mutate → reassemble RE tools IDA Pro, JEB3, Hopper, Ghidra Disassembly linear (sequential, fears embedded data) / recursive (follows the control flow) Decompilation disasm → variable/type → CFG → optimization → code generation Type inference *a pointer, %d integer, fopen string Cracking find cmp/serial → patch jne→jmp/nop; little-endian Anti-RE disassembly interference, obfuscation, packing

docs.title: Chapter 5 · Buffer Overflow & Obfuscation · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w5/buffer-overflow.pdf, w5/obfuscation.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 80 minutes + worked examples 40 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.7, §2.8

Weight of this chapter: the stack frame diagram + the overflow exploitation steps + the limitations of the three defenses are guaranteed exam focuses; obfuscation is more conceptual, and the "three kinds + four evaluation dimensions" is the usual question.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. C/C++ does no bounds checking + the stack grows toward low addresses → an over-long input overwrites the return address → a crash or control-flow hijacking (executing arbitrary code).
  2. Defense is "layered": W^X makes the stack non-executable, the canary detects the overrun, ASLR makes the address unguessable; every layer has a bypass, there is no silver bullet.
  3. Obfuscation is not encryption: it only changes the form of the code (layout/data/control flow), and the goal is to make the resources required for reversing it more expensive than the payoff; evaluation looks at potency / stealth / resilience / cost.

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Diagram Draw the stack frame and label buf/EBP/ret Memorize the "high address → low address" order Computation The offset for buf[64] to overwrite ret, the payload bytes Be able to compute 64+4 and to write an address in little-endian Defense analysis What NX/canary/ASLR each prevents, and how to bypass each Memorize the table Concepts The three kinds of obfuscation, the four evaluation dimensions Give 2 examples for each kind Design Why obfuscation cannot completely prevent RE Answer "cost + Kerckhoffs + limited search space"

docs.title: 1.1 The vulnerability spectrum and "exploitability"★
docs.text:
Bugs that can be potentially exploited (as listed in the slides):

  • Null pointer dereference, UAF, double free, array indexing errors, stack/heap overflow;
  • Return pointers to local variables, uninitialized variables, invalid use of negative values;
  • Passing large parameters by value, underallocations of dynamic data;
  • Memory/file handle/network resource leaks, unhandled return codes, use of invalid iterators.

⚠ Not all bugs are exploitable; logic bugs that are not exploitable do not constitute a vulnerability. Common high-risk ones: buffer overflow, format string, integer overflow, UAF, type confusion, race condition.

docs.title: 1.2 Process memory layout ★★
docs.text:
1High address
 2┌──────────────┐
 3│ stack        │ ← grows toward low addresses
 4├──────────────┤
 5│              │
 6├──────────────┤
 7│ heap         │ ← grows toward high addresses
 8├──────────────┤
 9│ bss          │ uninitialized globals/statics
10├──────────────┤
11│ data         │ initialized globals/statics
12├──────────────┤
13│ text         │ code
14└──────────────┘
15Low address
  • Mac/Windows are very similar; the concrete addresses are randomized (ASLR), which changes the base addresses.
  • A stack frame (32-bit, simplified, alignment padding ignored):
 1High address
 2┌─────────────────┐
 3│ parameters a, b │
 4├─────────────────┤
 5│ return address  │ ← overflow target (4 bytes)
 6├─────────────────┤
 7│ saved EBP       │ ← 4 bytes
 8├─────────────────┤
 9│ local variables │
10│ char buf[64]    │ ← write start, written toward high addresses
11└─────────────────┘
12Low address         ESP
  • When a function is called, the return address, the stack frame pointer, and the variables are pushed on the stack; the stack grows toward low addresses while the buffer is written toward high addresses → the overflow overwrites saved EBP first, then ret.

docs.title: 1.3 Two kinds of "out-of-bounds" ★
docs.text: Type Behavior Consequence Example Buffer overread Read beyond the buffer Leaks adjacent memory (can bypass ASLR) Heartbleed (OpenSSL overread) Buffer overwrite Write beyond the buffer Tampering with adjacent data/return address Stack overflow, heap overflow

docs.title: 1.4 How the overflow attack works ★★
docs.text:
The simplest scenario: next to char buffer[N] there is a boolean flag (the password-correct flag); an over-long input overwrites the flag → any password is accepted.

Stack overflow:

  1. Overwrite ret → the program "returns" to the wrong location → a crash (DoS);
  2. Worse: make ret point to injected malicious code (shellcode) → arbitrary code execution;
  3. Also known as: stack smashing, buffer overrun, code injection, control-flow hijacking.

Preconditions: - A buffer overflow must actually exist in the code; - Not all buffer overflows are exploitable; - Trial and error is usually needed to guess the address, but "one success is enough".

⚠ "What if buffer grows forwardly?" does not solve the problem (the slides say "see my notes") — because ret is still "above" the buffer; only the direction of the overwrite has changed, and the attacker can still construct a layout.

docs.title: 1.5 Unsafe C library functions ★
docs.text:
Function Problem strcpy(dest, src) Does not check the length of dest gets(s) Has no idea of the buffer size strcat(dest, src) May overrun when appending scanf("%s", ...) Does not limit the width sprintf(buf, ...) The formatted output may be over-long

The common problem: the length of the destination buffer is not checked; use the length-taking versions such as strncpy/snprintf/fgets, and check the return values.

docs.title: 1.6 Exploitation steps (the serial case) ★★
docs.text:
Scenario: the program asks for a serial number that you do not know, and you only have the executable (exe); it quits on an incorrect serial number.

  1. Discover the offset: by trial and error, feed A (0x41) with increasing length and observe whether ret is overwritten with 0x41414141 when it crashes → pin down the offset.
  2. Find the target address: disassemble the code and find the address that "skips the check" (e.g., 0x401034).
  3. Write the address in little-endian: 0x401034 → bytes 34 10 40 00 → ASCII 4^P@.
  4. Construct the payload: padding + target address (plus a NOP sled + shellcode if necessary).
  5. Trigger: when the program returns it jumps to the target address and bypasses the check.

Offset computation (32-bit, simplified):

1char buf[64];
2offset(ret) = 64 (buf) + 4 (saved EBP) = 68
3payload = b"A"*68 + p32(target)

If the target address contains 0x00, strcpy truncates it → a practical exploit must choose an address free of null bytes (e.g., 0x0804a080 → \x80\xa0\x04\x08), or use another way of writing.

NOP sled: put a large number of 0x90 bytes in front of the shellcode; as long as ret lands anywhere in the sled it slides into the shellcode, which lowers the difficulty of "guessing the address exactly".

docs.title: 1.7 Defenses ★★
docs.text:
Defense Mechanism What it prevents Limitation/bypass W^X / DEP Stack/heap marked as non-executable (write XOR execute) Direct execution of shellcode on the stack ROP/return-to-libc reuses existing code; JIT/self-modifying code needs writable and executable memory Canary A random value placed between the local variables and saved EBP; checked before the function returns Contiguous stack overflows (the canary must be destroyed to reach ret) The canary can be leaked (format string/info leak); an arbitrary write may leave the canary untouched; not fool-proof; about 8% performance penalty ASLR Randomizes the base addresses of the stack, heap, libraries, and executable Makes the attacker's address guess miss 32-bit entropy is low, so it can be brute-forced; spraying works; needs an info leak; does not prevent attacks that do not rely on a fixed address Safe languages Automatic bounds checking in Java/C#/Rust, etc. Removes out-of-bounds access at the root Requires rewriting/migration; performance, compatibility, FFI Safe functions Library functions with a length parameter + checks Reduces common mistakes Depends on the developer using them correctly; logic errors remain

Canary details

  • The classic constant 0x000aff0d (contains \x00, \x0a, \xff, \x0d, which prevents string functions from copying it by accident); a random value decided during runtime also works.
  • Pushed in the function prologue and compared in the epilogue; a mismatch → __stack_chk_fail → termination.
  • Bypass: leak the canary first and write it back unchanged; or use a write primitive that does not go through the stack.

ASLR details

  • The attacker can repetitively guess the randomized address (especially since the 32-bit address space is small); they can spray a large amount of attack code to raise the hit rate.
  • Combined with NX, attackers turn to ROP: stitching attack logic out of existing code fragments (gadgets).

The modern combination: ASLR + canary + NX + PIE + CFI; no single defense is enough.

docs.title: 1.8 Why "the buffer growing forwardly" is not the solution
docs.text:
• If the buffer grows toward high addresses, ret is on the low-address side and seems safe from being overwritten;
  • but the attacker can overwrite other critical data (function pointers, saved EBP, parameters), or use the heap/other structures;
  • the root problem is the lack of bounds checking, not the direction of growth.

docs.title: 2.1 Motivation and threat model ★
docs.text:
• Software contains code that is highly informative: MSIL for .NET, bytecode for Java/JS/Python, binary code for C/C++.
  • Code can be exploited:
  • Non-malicious RE: for testing, integration, extending;
  • Malicious RE: for security attacking, piracy, plagiarism;
  • malware authors also want to evade malware clustering/similarity analysis.
  • Mobile code + "malicious" hosts: the code runs on someone else's machine and the host is not trustworthy → "software protection" is needed.

docs.title: 2.2 Why existing protection is not enough ⚠
docs.text: Approach Problem Hardware isolation Retrofit hardware is needed; not viable Server-side execution Requires always-on high bandwidth; authentication and other network security problems also need to be taken care of Encryption Chicken-egg problem: the decryption routine itself is visible, so the attacker always ends up with the decrypted code

docs.title: 2.3 Goal and limits ★
docs.text:
• Obfuscation: making protected software "look" dissimilar to its original version; determining the "similarity" of two pieces of code is the building block of many software security analyses.
  • It can never completely protect an application from malicious RE: given sufficient time and resources, any obfuscated code can be reversed (exhaustive search).
  • The right goal: make the resources required for undoing the transforms too expensive for attackers (raise the cost instead of pursuing absolute security).

docs.title: (1) Layout obfuscation
docs.text:
• Comment stripping and identifier renaming (classes/methods/variables → meaningless names).
  • Tools: DashO (Java), Dotfuscator (MSIL).
  • Characteristics: very lightweight, does not change semantics; in the real world plenty of popular apps are not even layout obfuscated.

docs.title: (2) Data obfuscation
docs.text:
• Variable splitting, merging, and encoding.
  • Arrays split into several sub-arrays, two or more arrays merged into one bigger array, arrays folded so as to increase the number of dimensions, arrays flattened to decrease the number of dimensions.
  • Data encryption (e.g., string encryption, very common in mobile apps).
  • Goal: make it harder to infer "what the data is and how it is used".

docs.title: (3) Control-flow obfuscation ★
docs.text:
Premise: layout/data obfuscation does not change the control structure of the program → the control structure can still be leveraged as a code signature.

Method 1: instruction insertion (garbage code insertion)

  • Insert meaningless instructions or sequences of instructions: nop; or a semantically canceling sequence: add → sub, xor → xor.
  • Advantages: easy to implement, and can easily break known patterns/signatures.

Method 2: instruction replacement/substitution

  • Replace the original instructions with an equivalent sequence of instructions.
  • Extreme case: M/o/Vfuscator compiles C/C++ programs into mov instructions, and only "mov" instructions.

Method 3: control flow flattening

  • Put all the basic blocks of the function into a single switch(x) dispatcher, driven by the state variable x.
  • The original CFG is "flattened" and loses its obvious branch/loop structure.

Example: function f(i,j): a=1; if(i<j) a=j; do { a*=i--; } while(i>0); return a;

Original basic block State after flattening A: a=1 x=0 → case 0: A; x = (i<j) ? 1 : 2 B: a=j case 1: B; x=3 C: a=a*i; i=i-1 case 2: C; x = (i>0) ? 2 : 3 D: return a case 3: D

The outer layer keeps only a single while(true) switch(x).

Method 4: opaque predicates

  • The value of the conditional expression is known at runtime, but difficult for the adversary to deduce by statically analyzing the code.
  • Example: if (x*x + y*y >= 2*x*y) is always true, because \((x-y)^{2} \ge 0\); in assembly it is even less obvious.
  • Types:
  • Invariant: always true/always false, independent of the input;
  • Context: holds only in a specific context;
  • Multi-threading: one thread puts random numbers >n into a global data structure, another thread takes one of these numbers and assigns it to x → if (x<n) is always false.
  • The opacity property of predicates determines the resilience of control-flow transformations.

Advanced

  • VM-based obfuscation: invent new instruction sets with secret encodings + a virtual CPU/dispatcher; it has been commercialized; not a fool-proof technique, but it makes analysis significantly more difficult.
  • Multilingual obfuscation: "mixing" different computation models (imperative = Turing machine, functional = lambda calculus, logic = Horn logic); after translation and compilation the machine code is harder to understand.

docs.title: 2.5 Evaluating obfuscation effectiveness ★★
docs.text:
Dimension Meaning Measurement Potency How much complexity the obfuscation introduces Number of call graph edges, basic blocks, CFG edges, etc. Stealth How well obfuscated code blends in with the rest of the program Instruction distribution anomaly test Resilience How difficult it is to undo the obfuscation Diffing techniques to test similarity between obfuscated and original binaries Cost Performance penalty caused by obfuscation Size, execution slowdown

The four need to be traded off: high potency may mean high cost; good stealth may mean low resilience.

docs.title: 2.6 Why "good" obfuscation is hard to design ⚠
docs.text:
• Coming up with "interesting" obfuscation mutations is not too difficult, it requires some creativity; coming up with "secure" obfuscation mutations is very difficult.
  • Especially when people are aware of your obfuscation method (an extension of Kerckhoffs).
  • Open design with no real secret and a limited search space is not good in principle.

docs.title: Example 1: ret offset (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: In a 32-bit program, a function contains char buf[64], with no alignment padding; saved EBP is 4 bytes, ret is 4 bytes. How many bytes of padding are needed to overwrite ret?

Answer: - buf is 64 bytes; - saved EBP is 4 bytes; - therefore ret begins at byte 68 from the start of buf; - payload = b"A"*68 + p32(target).

Scoring points: state that "saved EBP is overwritten first, then ret"; mention that a real compiler may add alignment padding, which must be confirmed dynamically.

docs.title: Example 2: little-endian payload (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: The target address is 0x0804a080; write out the address bytes in the payload.

Answer: - little-endian: the low byte comes first → 80 a0 04 08; - Python: p32(0x0804a080) = b"\x80\xa0\x04\x08". - If the address contains \x00 (e.g., 0x08048400), strcpy truncates it; change the address or change the way of writing.

docs.title: Example 3: canary principle (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: How does the canary detect a stack overflow? How does the attacker bypass it?

Answer: - The compiler places a random value between the local variables and saved EBP; before the function returns it compares whether that value has been changed; a mismatch calls __stack_chk_fail and terminates. - A contiguous overflow must pass through the canary to reach ret, so it is detected. - Bypass: ① leak the canary and write it back unchanged (format string/info leak); ② use an arbitrary write that does not go through that stack frame; ③ overwrite a path that does not trigger the check.

docs.title: Example 4: the limits of ASLR (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: ASLR randomizes addresses, so why can a 32-bit program still be bypassed?

Answer: - The entropy of the 32-bit address space is limited, so the attacker can brute-force the guess (retry repeatedly, restarting after a crash); - heap/stack spraying can lay out a large amount of attack code/ROP gadgets to raise the hit rate; - an info leak is needed to disclose the base address; or the attacker turns to an attack that does not need a fixed address (e.g., partial overwrite). - Therefore ASLR must be combined with NX, canary, CFI, etc.

docs.title: Example 5: control flow flattening (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: Flatten a=1; if(i<j) a=j; do{a*=i--;}while(i>0); return a; with a switch dispatcher.

Answer:

1x = 0;
2while (1) {
3  switch (x) {
4    case 0: a = 1; x = (i < j) ? 1 : 2; break;
5    case 1: a = j; x = 3; break;
6    case 2: a = a * i; i = i - 1; x = (i > 0) ? 2 : 3; break;
7    case 3: return a;
8  }
9}
  • The branches/loops of the original CFG are "hidden" in the assignments to the state variable x; static analysis must first recover the values of x before it can rebuild the CFG.

docs.title: Example 6: opaque predicates (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: Why is if (x*x + y*y >= 2*x*y) always true? What is the precondition?

Answer: - \(x^{2} + y^{2} - 2xy = (x-y)^{2} \ge 0\); - therefore it is always true for any real numbers x and y; in assembly it is not easy to see. - Precondition: the integer arithmetic does not overflow; if it overflows the predicate may be false (this must be considered at design time).

docs.title: Example 7: evaluating obfuscation (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: An obfuscator makes a program 3× larger and 40% slower to run, but its instruction distribution differs clearly from normal code. Evaluate it with the four dimensions.

Answer: - Cost: poor (3× size, 40% slower); - Stealth: poor (the instruction distribution is anomalous and easily caught by statistical detection); - Potency: need to see whether the CFG/basic block complexity really increases; - Resilience: need diffing/similarity analysis to see how hard it is to undo. - Conclusion: this obfuscation is "visually complex", but stealth and cost are unsatisfactory, so the overall effect is limited.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes (where points are lost most easily)
docs.text: Mistake Correct The stack grows toward high addresses The stack grows toward low addresses; the buffer is written toward high addresses An overflow always overwrites ret It may only overwrite local variables/EBP; it depends on the layout and the length All overflows are exploitable Many only cause a crash; exploitability depends on the layout, the address, and the protections NX prevents all code execution It prevents "execution on the stack"; ROP/return-to-libc bypasses it The canary is fool-proof It can be leaked/bypassed; it does not protect non-contiguous writes ASLR makes attacks impossible 32-bit can be brute-forced; spraying works; an info leak is needed Using safe functions makes you safe Logic errors and length-computation errors remain Obfuscation = encryption Obfuscation does not keep secrets, it only raises the cost of understanding; encryption has a key Obfuscation can completely prevent RE It cannot; it can only raise the cost The higher the potency the better The trade-off with stealth/resilience/cost also matters Control flow flattening changes the program semantics It does not; it only hides the CFG in the state variable

docs.title: 5. Self-test (do it first, then look at the answers)
docs.text:
1. Draw a 32-bit stack frame and label the order of the parameters, ret, saved EBP, and buf.
  2. Why can an overflow overwrite the return address? In which direction does the stack grow?
  3. What is the difference between overread and overwrite? Which one is Heartbleed?
  4. List 5 unsafe C library functions and explain their common problem.
  5. Describe the complete exploitation steps of a stack overflow; what is the role of the NOP sled?
  6. What does each of W^X, canary, and ASLR prevent? What is each one's limitation?
  7. Why does "letting the buffer grow toward high addresses" not solve the problem?
  8. What are the three kinds of obfuscation? Give two concrete methods for each.
  9. What is the principle of control flow flattening? What is the essence of an opaque predicate?
  10. On which four dimensions is obfuscation effectiveness evaluated? Why is "secure obfuscation" hard?
  11. What are VM-based obfuscation and multilingual obfuscation?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. High → low: parameters, ret, saved EBP, local variables (buf is at the low-address end, closest to ESP).
  2. The stack grows toward low addresses and buf is written toward high addresses; ret is above buf, so an over-long write passes saved EBP first and then reaches ret.
  3. overread reads out of bounds (leak), overwrite writes out of bounds (tampering); Heartbleed is an overread.
  4. strcpy, gets, strcat, scanf("%s"), sprintf; none of them checks the length of the destination buffer.
  5. Discover the offset → find the target address → write the address in little-endian → construct the payload (padding + address, optionally with a NOP sled/shellcode) → trigger the return. The NOP sled lowers the precision required of the address guess.
  6. W^X: the stack is non-executable, preventing shellcode; it can be bypassed by ROP. canary: detects contiguous overflows; it can be leaked/bypassed. ASLR: randomizes addresses; 32-bit can be brute-forced and sprayed.
  7. The root problem is the lack of bounds checking; ret can still be overwritten through another layout/structure, or function pointers/parameters can be changed.
  8. Layout (renaming, comment stripping); data (array splitting/merging, string encryption); control flow (garbage instructions, instruction substitution, flattening, opaque predicates).
  9. Put all basic blocks into a switch dispatcher driven by a state variable; an opaque predicate is a conditional whose "value is known at runtime but difficult to deduce statically".
  10. Potency, Stealth, Resilience, Cost; because the method is open (Kerckhoffs), there is no real secret and the search space is limited, so an attacker can reverse it in a targeted way.
  11. VM-based: a custom instruction set + a virtual CPU interpreting it; multilingual: mixing different computation models such as imperative/functional/logic.

docs.title: 6. Pre-exam quick-reference card
docs.text: Item Content Stack direction The stack grows toward low addresses; buf is written toward high addresses 32-bit stack frame parameters / ret / saved EBP / buf (low address) Offset buf[64] → ret offset 68 (64+4) Little-endian The low byte comes first; 0x0804a080 → 80 a0 04 08 Dangerous functions strcpy, gets, strcat, scanf, sprintf Aliases stack smashing, code injection, control-flow hijacking W^X The stack is non-executable; bypass: ROP/return-to-libc Canary 0x000aff0d or random; about 8% overhead; can be leaked ASLR Randomizes base addresses; low 32-bit entropy; can be sprayed/brute-forced Three kinds of obfuscation layout / data / control-flow Control-flow methods garbage instructions, instruction substitution (mov-only), flattening, opaque predicates Opaque predicates \((x-y)^{2}\ge 0\); invariant/context/multi-threading Evaluation potency / stealth / resilience / cost Limits Obfuscation only raises the cost; it cannot completely prevent RE

docs.title: Chapter 6 · Software Exploitation II & Side Channels · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w6/attack2.pdf, w6/side-channel.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 90 minutes + worked examples 30 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.9, §2.10

Weight of this chapter: the "cause + exploit + defense" of UAF/double free/format string/SQLi is the focus of short-answer/design questions; side channels usually test the "three conditions + RSA timing/cache/power".

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. The essence of heap vulnerabilities is a "lifecycle/type management failure": use after free (UAF), freeing twice (double free), treating type A as type B (type confusion).
  2. A format string is "treating user input as code": %s leaks memory, %n writes to an arbitrary address; SQL injection is "treating user input as syntax": concatenating strings changes the semantics of the query.
  3. Side channels do not exploit software bugs, they exploit the chain "secret-dependent program behavior → physical effect → observable": time, cache, power, EM emissions, sound, heat.

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Cause analysis How does a UAF arise? Why is it dangerous? Draw the "free → reuse" timeline Exploit reasoning What can %n do? What about %s? Distinguish "read" from "write" Defense design How to prevent SQLi/format string/UAF Memorize 2–3 items for each vulnerability Side channel The three conditions? The principle of the RSA timing attack? Memorize the timing of square-and-multiply Cache How does Flush+Reload work? Strong or weak threat model? Draw the cache line + address split

docs.title: 1.1 Heap basics ★
docs.text:
• Heap: the portion of memory where dynamically allocated memory resides; C uses malloc/free, C++ uses new/delete.
  • Memory allocated from the heap remains allocated until the program terminates or it is explicitly freed/deleted.
  • Programmers need to take care of the lifecycle → a breeding ground for bugs.
  • Memory leak: allocate without freeing → resource abuse → crash/lost response → breaks Availability.

docs.title: 1.2 Use-After-Free (UAF) ★★
docs.text:
Definition: after the program calls free(p), it still reads and writes through p, treating the freed memory as valid.

Why it is dangerous

1User *u = malloc(sizeof(User));
2...
3free(u);
4Service *s = malloc(sizeof(Service));  // very likely reuses the same chunk of memory
5strcpy(s->name, attacker_data);          // write through s
6login(u);                                // still reads through the dangling pointer u → reads attacker_data
  • A freed chunk is reused by the allocator; the new object occupies the same address.
  • The attacker controls the contents of the new object → through the dangling pointer they read/write the fields of the "new object" (function pointers, permission flags, vtable) → control-flow hijacking/privilege escalation.

The Protostar heap2 case (PoC)

Normal flow:

11. create user   (strdup allocates the username)
22. login
33. specify service (strdup allocates the service name)
44. cleanup (free the user)

Attack flow:

11. create user
22. cleanup (free the user, but the pointer is not nulled)
33. specify service (a new strdup reuses the same chunk and writes "you have already logged in!")
44. login (still uses the old user pointer → reads what the attacker wrote)
  • Result: "already logged in" without authentication.
  • Key: the size strdup allocates equals that of the user → the same chunk is reused.

Why fuzz testing finds it difficult to detect: complexity + saliency — it needs a specific allocate/free/reallocate sequence, which random mutation rarely hits.

Prevention

  • Set all freed pointers to NULL (the most direct);
  • Use smart pointers (C++ unique_ptr/shared_ptr), GC;
  • Allocator isolation/delayed reuse (hardening).

docs.title: 1.3 Double Free ★
docs.text:
Definition: the same block of memory is freed twice.

Impact: the heap allocator manages memory through chunk headers/free lists; the second free parses "user data" as metadata → heap metadata is corrupted → an arbitrary address write/control-flow hijacking can be constructed.

Typical exploit:

1free(R1);                 // R1 enters the free list
2R2 = malloc(same_size);   // reuses R1
3write(R2, data);          // control the data
4free(R1);                 // free again: parses R2's data as metadata
5free(R2);                 // messes things up further

Prevention: set the pointer to NULL after freeing (the most direct); avoid double-free paths; use smart pointers.

docs.title: 1.4 Type confusion (for awareness)
docs.text:
• Using an object of one type as another type (e.g., treating an int as a pointer, or a parent class as a child class).
  • Common in C++ casts, unions, and deserialization; can lead to out-of-bounds read/write/control-flow hijacking.
  • The slides only name it without elaborating; knowing that "type confusion is a memory safety vulnerability" is enough.

docs.title: 2.1 Principle
docs.text:
1printf(const char *format, ...);
  • The format string determines how the subsequent arguments are interpreted: %d as an integer, %s as a pointer whose target string is printed, %n writes.
  • Traditionally, compilers do not check whether the number/type of arguments matches the format string.
  • If the user can control the format string:
1printf(user_input);   // dangerous!

docs.title: 2.2 Two exploits
docs.text:
(1) %s: information leak

  • printf("%s%s%s...") takes the values on the stack in turn as string addresses and prints what they point to → leaks memory (stack, libc, canary, return address).
  • Can be used to bypass ASLR.

(2) %n: arbitrary memory write

  • %n writes "the number of bytes written via the format string processing up to that point" to the address specified by the argument.
  • The attacker controls the format string + arguments → a controlled value can be written to an arbitrary address (width modifiers control the value written).
  • This is the most dangerous consequence of a format string: arbitrary write → control-flow hijacking.

Small example

1int n;
2printf("AAAA%n", &n);   // n = 4 (4 bytes written so far)
3printf("%100c%n", 'A', &n); // n = 100

docs.title: 2.3 Prevention ★
docs.text:
• Do not use user input directly as the format string: printf("%s", user_input).
  • Use hard-coded format strings whenever possible, with a matching number/type of arguments.
  • Do not use %n (compiler option/security library).
  • Compiler warnings (-Wformat-security), code audit.

docs.title: 3.1 Principle
docs.text:
1$query = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE name='$name';";
  • User input is pasted verbatim into the SQL string → quotes/keywords in the input change the query structure.

Classic payloads

Input Generated SQL Effect x' OR 'a'='a ... WHERE name='x' OR 'a'='a'; always true, bypasses login '; DROP TABLE Students; -- ...; DROP TABLE Students; -- drops the table (whether it executes depends on whether the API supports multiple statements)

docs.title: 3.2 Best defense: prepared statements + bound variables ★★
docs.text:
