1$sth = $dbh->prepare("SELECT email, userid FROM members WHERE email = ?;");
2$sth->execute($email);

Why it works:

  1. The SQL statement is first parsed and compiled by the database (at this point ? is a parameter placeholder);
  2. The parameter values are then combined with the "compiled statement";
  3. The input is always treated as data and is never parsed as SQL syntax.

Key sentence: "The parameter values are combined with the compiled statement, not a SQL string."

docs.title: 3.3 Other defenses
docs.text:
• Check the syntax of input for validity: email addresses, dates, part numbers, etc. have fixed languages; verify with a whitelist/regex.
  • Length limits: many injections depend on entering long strings.
  • Keyword scanning: INSERT, DROP, etc., but beware of false positives (valid user input may legitimately contain them).
  • Least database privileges: grant read-only accounts only SELECT; do not use root for the application account.
  • Do not echo error messages (avoids leaking the table structure).

docs.title: 4.1 The three conditions ★★
docs.text:
1. Secret-dependent program information flow: the program's behavior differs with the secret (branches, memory access, amount of computation).
  2. The information flow affects the physical environment: time, power, cache status, EM emissions, sound, heat.
  3. The physical environment is observable/exploitable by the attacker.

All three are required; defense also starts from these three rings: eliminate secret-dependent behavior (constant time), shield the physical signal (masking/noise reduction), limit observation (isolation/exclusive use).

docs.title: 4.2 Types
docs.text: Type Leak source Example Timing execution time the "fast/slow" branches of RSA square & multiply Cache cache hit/miss Flush+Reload observes which cache line the victim accessed Power power consumption SPA reads the key bits from one power trace EM EM emissions collected with a near-field probe Sound sound CPU humming/keyboard clicks; slide example: the hum spectrum differs for different key bits Heat heat thermal imaging

docs.title: 4.3 RSA timing side channel ★★
docs.text:
Scenario

  • Alice's public key (N,e), private key d; the attacker can send any M and Alice responds with \(M^d \bmod N\) (a signature); the attacker can precisely time it.

Implementation: square & multiply

1for bit in d:            # from the most significant bit to the least significant bit
2    x = x² mod N
3    if bit == 1:
4        x = x*M mod N

Timing difference

  • bit = 0: square only → fast;
  • bit = 1: square + multiply → slow.

Attack: measure the total time of each signature and recover the bit sequence of d from the "fast/slow" pattern.

  • A single trace is usually not enough (noise, scheduling); a considerable number of trials and statistics are needed; but there is no need to factor large numbers.
  • Classic reference: Kocher 1996.

Why it is dangerous: RSA's private-key operation naturally has "secret-dependent branches"; implementation optimizations (such as Montgomery multiplication) may also show timing differences.

docs.title: 4.4 Cache side channel ★★
docs.text:
Basic principle

  • Accessing data stored in the cache is measurably faster than accessing the data from main memory.
  • Cache lines are the minimal storage units of a cache, usually 64 bytes.
  • Address split (simplified):
131                6 5      0
2[   cache line index  ][offset]
  • Different variables in the same line are brought into the cache together; accesses to different lines can be distinguished.

Flush + Reload

  1. The attacker evicts (flushes) the target cache line;
  2. Wait for the victim to execute;
  3. The attacker reloads that line and measures the time:
    • fast → the victim accessed it (the line is in the cache);
    • slow → the victim did not access it (it must be fetched from memory).

Threat model

Strength Capability Strong can observe which particular cache line the victim accessed Weak can only observe the hit/miss sequence, yet can still infer the secret input

Relation to RSA

  • Square & multiply: secret-dependent control flow → timing/branch leakage;
  • Sliding window: idx = window(key,i); t = table[idx] → secret-dependent memory access → cache leakage.

Why it is especially dangerous in the cloud

  • Different VMs share the same cache: instances on the same core share L1/L2, instances across cores share L3.
  • The attacker only needs co-residency with the victim to observe.
  • Related big event: 2018 Spectre & Meltdown (speculative execution + cache side channel).

docs.title: 4.5 Power side channel ★
docs.text:
SPA (Simple Power Analysis)

  • Directly interprets the power trace, identifying the operations taking place on the device and the key bits.
  • Assumption: the attacker can get a power trace, representing a set of power consumptions across a cryptographic process.
  • One trace is enough to reveal the secret (different operations/bits correspond to different power waveforms).
  • There are already PoC attacks on mobile phone and embedded devices.

Advanced DPA (differential power analysis), masking, hiding, etc. are not covered by the slides; knowing SPA's "one trace" characteristic is enough.

docs.title: 4.6 Defense ideas (supplementary, usable in answers)
docs.text: Level Measure Algorithm implementation Constant time: no secret-dependent branches, no secret-dependent array indices; fixed order Randomization Blinding: RSA message blinding \(M' = M\cdot r^e\), exponent blinding; avoid identical inputs Power masking, hiding, dual-rail logic Cache disable shared memory/cache coloring, flush, isolate cores System exclusive physical cores, disable hyper-threading, trusted execution environment

docs.title: Example 1: UAF exploitation (10 points)
docs.text:
Question:

1struct User { char name[16]; int is_admin; };
2struct User *u = malloc(sizeof(struct User));
3strcpy(u->name, "bob"); u->is_admin = 0;
4free(u);
5struct Service *s = malloc(sizeof(struct Service)); // same size
6strcpy(s->name, "...."); // attacker-controlled
7if (u->is_admin) { /* admin operation */ }

Explain how to escalate privileges with the UAF.

Answer: - After free(u), u is not nulled; malloc(Service) very likely reuses the same chunk. - The attacker makes s->name overwrite the original User's is_admin field (same layout/controllable offset), writing 1 into it. - Afterwards u->is_admin reads 1 → it executes as an administrator. - Prevention: free(u); u = NULL;; use smart pointers; allocator isolation.

docs.title: Example 2: Format string (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: printf(buf), where buf is controlled by the user. What can %s and %n each do? How do you prevent it?

Answer: - %s: takes the values on the stack as string addresses and prints their contents → information leak (can leak the canary/return address/libc address, bypassing ASLR). - %n: writes the number of bytes written so far to the address specified by the argument → arbitrary write (can change the GOT/return address/permission variables). - Prevention: printf("%s", buf); hard-coded format strings; do not use %n; compiler warnings.

docs.title: Example 3: SQL injection (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: The login query is SELECT * FROM Users WHERE name='$name' AND pwd='$pwd'. Give a payload that bypasses it, and explain why a prepared statement prevents it.

Answer: - name = ' OR '1'='1' -- → the query becomes ... WHERE name='' OR '1'='1' -- ' AND pwd='...', always true. - Prepared statement: the SQL is compiled first and ? is a parameter placeholder; the input is bound only as data and is never parsed as SQL syntax. - Also: least privilege, input validation, length limits, no error message echo.

docs.title: Example 4: RSA timing attack (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: The measured times of four signatures are "slow, fast, slow, slow"; what are the corresponding key bits of square & multiply?

Answer: - slow = square + multiply = 1; fast = square only = 0; - the sequence is 1 0 1 1. - Precondition: timing precise enough and noise controllable; in practice many trials are needed.

docs.title: Example 5: Cache line (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: int A[100], cache line 64 bytes, base address of A 64-byte aligned. Are A[10] and A[50] in the same cache line?

Answer: - each int is 4 bytes; A[10] is at offset 40 → line 0; A[50] is at offset 200 → 200/64 = 3 → line 3. - They are not in the same line; the attacker flushes line 0, waits for the victim to run and reloads: fast = the victim accessed A[10] (the line is in the cache), slow = it did not. - This shows that when the array index is a secret (e.g., the AES S-box, the RSA window table), the cache leaks the index.

docs.title: Example 6: SPA (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: Why does SPA need only one power trace?

Answer: - Different operations (e.g., square vs. multiply) have different power waveforms; the key bits correspond directly to the operation sequence. - One trace covering the whole computation already contains the "operation sequence" information; no statistics over a large number of samples is needed (only DPA needs that).

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes (where points are lost most easily)
docs.text: Mistake Correct UAF and double free are the same thing UAF is "use after free"; double free is "freeing twice"; they can be related but are different The pointer automatically becomes NULL after freeing C free does not null it; you must set it to NULL manually A memory leak directly leaks data A leak is resource exhaustion (availability); "leaking data" is an information leak %s writes and %n reads The other way round: %s reads (prints a string), %n writes printf(buf) and printf("%s", buf) are the same The former treats buf as the format string, the latter as data; the former is dangerous Escaping quotes is enough to prevent SQLi Not thorough; use prepared statements + least privilege A prepared statement is just "escaping" It "compiles the statement first, then binds the data"; the input takes no part in syntax parsing Side channels need a software vulnerability No; they exploit the implementation's behavior/physical leakage Side channels are only timing There are also cache, power, EM, sound, heat A cache attack needs to read the victim's memory No; it only observes the cache status (hit/miss/line) VMs isolated in the cloud have no side channel Shared cache/CPU still leaks (same core L1/L2, cross core L3) Constant time = short code It means "execution time is independent of the secret", not "fast"

docs.title: 7. Self-test (do it first, then look at the answers)
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between the heap and the stack? How do malloc/free and new/delete correspond?
  2. What causes a UAF and how is it exploited? How do you fix it?
  3. How does a double free mess up the heap? How do you prevent it?
  4. What do %s and %n each do in a format string? How do you prevent it?
  5. What is the principle of SQL injection? Why can a prepared statement prevent it?
  6. What other SQLi defenses are there? What are their limitations?
  7. What are the three conditions that form a side channel attack?
  8. Why does RSA square & multiply leak key bits? How do you recover them from the trace?
  9. What is the principle of Flush+Reload? What is the difference between the strong and weak threat models?
  10. Why does the cloud environment amplify cache side channel risk?
  11. What is the difference between SPA and DPA (for awareness)? Why is one trace enough for SPA?
  12. What are the defense ideas for side channels?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. The stack is allocated/freed automatically and holds local variables/return addresses; the heap is allocated manually and its lifecycle is controlled by the programmer. malloc↔free, new↔delete.
  2. After free the pointer is not nulled, so the dangling pointer can still read and write; the new allocation reuses the same chunk and the attacker controls its contents → the new object's fields/function pointers are tampered with. Fix: set to NULL, smart pointers, allocator isolation.
  3. The second free parses user data as allocator metadata and corrupts the free list → arbitrary write/control flow. Prevention: set to NULL, avoid double frees, smart pointers.
  4. %s uses a stack value as an address and reads a string from it (leak); %n writes the number of bytes written so far to the address given by the argument (arbitrary write). Prevention: hard-coded format strings, printf("%s", buf), do not use %n.
  5. User input pasted into the SQL changes the syntax (' OR '1'='1). A prepared statement compiles the SQL first and binds the parameters only as data, so the input takes no part in parsing.
  6. Input validation (may produce false positives/be bypassed), length limits (not thorough), keyword scanning (false positives), least privilege (limits the scope of impact), turning off error echo.
  7. Secret-dependent behavior, affecting the physical environment, being observable.
  8. bit=0 squares only (fast), bit=1 squares + multiplies (slow); measuring the time sequence gives the bit sequence (many trials needed).
  9. The attacker flushes the target line, waits for the victim to run, then reloads and measures the time; fast = it was accessed. The strong model can see the particular line, the weak model only hit/miss.
  10. Different VMs share L1/L2/L3; co-residency lets the attacker observe the victim's cache behavior.
  11. SPA reads the operations/key bits directly from one trace; DPA needs a large number of traces for statistics. SPA relies on the power difference between operations being clear.
  12. Constant time, blinding, masking/hiding, cache isolation/flush, exclusive cores/disabling hyper-threading, TEE.

docs.title: 8. Pre-exam quick-reference card
docs.text: Item Content Heap malloc/free, new/delete; leak → availability UAF use after free; chunk reuse; Protostar heap2; prevention: set to NULL/smart pointers Double free metadata corruption; prevention: set to NULL Format string %s leaks, %n arbitrary write; prevention: hard-coded format string, no %n SQLi ' OR '1'='1' --; prevention: prepared statement + least privilege The three conditions of a side channel secret-dependent behavior, physical effect, observable RSA timing square & multiply; 0 = fast (square), 1 = slow (square + multiply) Cache 64B line; Flush+Reload; hit is fast, miss is slow Cloud shared L1/L2/L3 → co-residency attacks Spectre/Meltdown 2018; speculative execution + cache side channel SPA one power trace reads the key Defense constant time, blinding, masking, isolation

docs.title: Chapter 7 · Authentication & Network Security · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: w7/authentication.pdf, w7/network-security.pdf

Suggested time: first pass 90 minutes + worked examples 30 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §2.11, §2.12

Weight of this chapter: authentication factors, password entropy/salting, and biometric error rates are short-answer/computation questions; the network part is almost entirely the mapping "layering + protocol + attack", which suits comprehensive questions.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. Access control = authentication (who you are) + authorization (what you can do); authentication relies on "something you know / something you have / something you are".
  2. The weakness of passwords is user choice (not length itself); hashing + salt turns an offline dictionary attack from "one-time precomputation" into "recomputation for every user". Biometrics are hard to forge, but cannot be revoked.
  3. A network is a layered, packet-switched protocol stack; each layer has its own address and protocols, and its own attack surface: application-layer spoofing, transport-layer DoS, network-layer IP (Internet Protocol)/NAT, link-layer ARP spoofing.

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Concept discrimination Authentication vs authorization; the three factors Give 3 examples for each factor Computation Password entropy, attack volume after salt, EER Be able to compute log2; be able to compare Protocols TCP three-way handshake, DNS resolution, NAT Draw the sequence/table Attacks SYN flood, DNS poisoning, ARP poisoning Memorize by "layer + root cause + defense" Design How to design a secure login / prevent replay Combine password + salt + 2FA + rate limiting

docs.title: 1.1 The two parts of access control ★
docs.text:
Concept Question Example Authentication Are you who you say you are? Login, fingerprint unlock, certificate verification Authorization Are you allowed to do that? A normal user cannot drop the database; RBAC/ACL
  • Authentication can be human-to-machine, and also machine-to-machine (e.g., TLS certificates).
  • Authenticate first, authorize second; if authentication fails, you should not reach the authorization check.

docs.title: 1.2 The three authentication factors ★★
docs.text:
Factor Meaning Example Advantage Disadvantage Something you know Something you know Password, PIN, date of birth, mother's maiden name, pet's name Free, easy to reset Weak, guessable, can leak, can be shared Something you have Something you have Smartcard, ATM card, token, cell phone, MAC address Requires physical possession, hard to copy remotely Can be lost, needs issuance/management Something you are Something you are Fingerprint, face, voiceprint, signature, gait Hard to forge, nothing to remember Cannot be revoked, has an error rate, collection needs cooperation

2FA (2-factor authentication): any two of the three categories. - Example: credit card + signature; ATM card + PIN; password + SMS code.

docs.title: Why passwords are popular
docs.text:
• Cost: passwords are free;
  • Convenience: it is easier to reset a password than to issue a new thumb;
  • But the slides quote: "Passwords are one of the biggest practical problems facing security engineers today."

docs.title: Keys vs passwords (key computation)
docs.text:
Key Password How it is generated Random Chosen by a person 64-bit key \(2^{64}\) keys, the attacker tries about \(2^{63}\) — 8 characters, 256 options per character Theoretically 256⁸ = \(2^{64}\) But users do not choose at random → in practice far less than \(2^{63}\) Attack method Brute force Dictionary attack
  • Dictionary attack: tries only the most likely candidates (dictionary words, mutations, common combinations).
  • Example: 8 lowercase letters → 26⁸ ≈ \(2^{37}\)·⁶; 8 printable characters (95 options) → 95⁸ ≈ \(2^{52}\)·⁶.

docs.title: Good and bad passwords, and passphrases
docs.text:
Bad passwords: frank, Fido, Password, incorrect, Pikachu, 88195277, AustinStamp. Good passwords: jfIej,43j-EmmL+y, 09864376537263, 0nceuP0nAt1m8, P0kem0n.

Passphrase:

  • 10–30 letters long, which makes brute force attacks difficult;
  • if well chosen, it will not be found in any phrase or quote dictionary;
  • structured to be more memorable than a random string.

Slide experiment (three groups of users)

Group Requirement Share cracked Memorability A At least 6 chars, 1 non-letter About 30% Average B Based on a passphrase About 10% Easy C 8 random characters About 10% Hard

Conclusion: a passphrase is the better trade-off between security and memorability; complexity requirements of the "add one special character" kind have limited effect.

docs.title: Password attack surface
docs.text:
• Target one particular account / any account on the system / any account on any system;
  • DoS: repeated wrong entries lock the account (think of the ATM swallowing your card);
  • Offline: dictionary/brute-force attack after obtaining the password hash file;
  • Online: guessing, credential stuffing, phishing, social engineering, keystroke logging;
  • Error logs may contain "almost" passwords; default passwords are not changed.

docs.title: Password storage: hashing + salt ★★
docs.text:
The problem with hashing only (no salt)

  1. The attacker precomputes h(x) (for every password in the dictionary) → one-time precomputation, after which comparing hashes breaks passwords in seconds;
  2. The same password → the same hash → accounts can be identified in bulk.

Salting (salt)

Choose a random \(s\); store \((s,\ y = h(\text{password}, s))\).

  • s is not secret; it can be stored together with y;
  • Verification: recompute h(input, s) with the stored s and compare it with y;
  • The attacker must recompute for every user and every salt, so the precomputed table is useless;
  • Cost: the offline attack goes from |D| to \(|D| \times \text{number of users}\) (plus the per-call cost of a slow hash).

Modern practice also uses a slow hash (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) to increase the cost of a single computation; the slides do not elaborate, but you may mention it in an answer.

docs.title: Other password issues
docs.text:
• Too many passwords → reuse → one leak compromises everything;
  • Default passwords are not changed;
  • Social engineering;
  • Login password vs ATM PIN are mixed up;
  • Keystroke logging/spyware;
  • Cracking tools: L0phtCrack/LC4 (Windows), John the Ripper (Unix); administrators should proactively audit weak passwords.

docs.title: Ideal properties
docs.text: Property Meaning Reality Universal Applies to (almost) everyone No biometric applies to everyone Distinguishing Distinguishes with certainty Cannot hope for 100% certainty Permanent Never changes over a lifetime It is OK if it remains valid for a long time Collectable Easy to collect the required data Depends on whether subjects are cooperative Safe, user-friendly — Must be traded off

docs.title: Enrollment vs Recognition
docs.text: Phase Requirement Risk Enrollment Biometric info is put into the database; may be slow and require repeated measurement; must be very precise The enrollment step may be a weak point (root trust) Recognition Must be quick and simple, yet reasonably accurate False rejection/false acceptance

docs.title: Error rates: fraud vs insult ★★
docs.text:
• Fraud: the attacker is mis-authenticated as Alice (the impostor is accepted).
  • Insult: Alice is not authenticated as Alice (the genuine user is rejected).
  • The two trade off against each other:
  • High threshold (99% match) → low fraud, high insult;
  • Low threshold (30% match) → high fraud, low insult.
  • EER (Equal Error Rate): the threshold point where fraud = insult; used to compare different biometrics, the smaller the better.

⚠ The slides label fraud as "false negative" and insult as "false positive", which is the opposite of the usual terminology; memorize by the definition: impostor accepted = fraud, genuine user rejected = insult.

docs.title: Biometrics are not foolproof
docs.text:
• An attacker can steal a thumb, photocopy a fingerprint/iris, 3D-print a mask;
  • An attacker can subvert the software/database/trusted base (TCB);
  • There is no way to revoke a "leaked" fingerprint — this is the biggest difference from passwords (a password can be changed, a fingerprint cannot).

docs.title: 1.5 2FA and the "have" factor
docs.text:
• 2FA: any combination of two categories of factors.
  • Examples of "have": car key, laptop (MAC address), password generator, ATM card, smartcard.
  • Note: an SMS code counts as "have the phone", but there is a SIM swap/interception risk (the slides do not elaborate).

docs.title: 2.1 Basic concepts ★
docs.text:
• A network = hosts (computer/laptop/server/phone) + an interconnected mesh of routers; the purpose is to transmit data.
  • Packet switched vs circuit switched:
  • The telephone network is circuit switched: for each call a dedicated circuit is established, which wastes bandwidth;
  • Data networks are packet switched: data is chopped up into packets that are transmitted independently, with no dedicated circuit; more efficient bandwidth usage, but more complex.
  • Protocols: precisely specify the "communication rules"; the details are given in RFCs (essentially Internet standards).
  • Stateless vs stateful: stateless protocols do not "remember", stateful ones do; many security problems are related to state (e.g., DoS is a problem with stateful protocols).

docs.title: 2.2 The five-layer protocol stack ★★
docs.text:
Layer Example protocols Role Address Application HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS Application semantics Domain name/URL Transport TCP, UDP End-to-end delivery Port (16 bit) Network IP, RIP/OSPF/BGP Routing/addressing IP (32 bit) Link Ethernet, PPP, 802.11 Transfer between adjacent nodes MAC (48 bit) Physical — Bit stream —

Layering in action

  • At the source, data goes "down" the protocol stack, and each layer adds a header;
  • A router processes a packet only "up" to the network layer (that is where the routing info lives), then passes it down the stack again;
  • The destination processes it "up" to the application layer.

Encapsulation

1Application layer: (H, X)
2Transport layer: (H, (H, X))
3Network layer: (H, (H, (H, X)))
4Link layer: (H, (H, (H, (H, X))))
  • The application data is on the "inside"; each layer's header is understood only by the peer layer.

docs.title: 2.3 Application layer ★
docs.text:
HTTP

  • Request/response; HTTP is stateless.
  • The client "speaks first" and the server responds (client-server); in P2P, hosts act as both client and server.

Cookie

  • Initially, the cookie is sent from the server to the browser; the browser stores it and sends it back on later requests;
  • The server uses a cookie database to "remember" you (shopping carts, recommendations, sessions);
  • A very (very) weak form of authentication;
  • Privacy concerns: one web site can learn a lot about you, and multiple web sites could learn even more (tracking).

SMTP

  • SMTP is used to deliver email from the sender to the recipient's mail server; then POP3/IMAP/HTTP is used to get the messages.
  • The commands are human readable:
1telnet server 25
2HELO ca.gov
3MAIL FROM: <arnold@ca.gov>
4RCPT TO: <stamp@cs.sjsu.edu>
5DATA
6...
7.
8QUIT
  • ⚔ Spoofed sender: MAIL FROM can be written at will → email spoofing.
  • Defense: SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication (not covered in the slides; supplementary).

DNS

  • Domain name → IP (cse.ust.hk → 143.89.41.177); a distributed database.
  • Resolution: root → TLD (.hk/.org/.edu) → sub-domain, performed recursively.
  • There are only 13 "root" DNS server clusters worldwide → essentially a single point of failure for the Internet; attacks on root servers have occurred, but did not last long enough.
  • ⚔ DNS cache poisoning: for performance, a server caches translations; if it receives and caches a false record, it returns the wrong IP to clients → traffic is diverted to the attacker's machine.
  • Defense: DNSSEC, randomizing the query ID/port, 0x20 encoding (not covered in the slides).

docs.title: 2.4 Transport layer ★
docs.text:
• The network layer offers unreliable, "best effort" delivery; any improved service must be provided by the hosts (transport layer).
  • TCP: reliable, in-order, flow control, connection-oriented (it contacts the server before sending data; a logical connection, not a physical one).
  • Header: source/destination port, sequence number, acknowledgment number, flags (ACK/SYN/RST...), window, checksum, urgent pointer; 20 bytes when there are no options.
  • Three-way handshake:
1Client → Server: SYN
2Server → Client: SYN-ACK
3Client → Server: ACK (and data)
  • ⚔ SYN flooding:
  • Whenever a SYN packet is received, the server remembers this "half-open" connection → this consumes resources (backlog);
  • Too many half-open connections → memory/table exhaustion → the server cannot respond to legitimate requests;
  • Root cause: TCP is stateful.
  • Defense: SYN cookies, rate limiting, firewall, shorter timeouts (not covered in the slides).
  • UDP: connectionless, low overhead, no guarantee of reliability/ordering.

docs.title: 2.5 Network layer ★
docs.text:
• IP: best effort; IP runs in every host and every router; routers also run routing protocols (RIP/OSPF/BGP).
  • An IPv4 address is 32 bits, in dotted decimal notation (195.72.180.27, each number between 0 and 255); not enough IP addresses → lots of tricks to extend the address space; a host's IP address can change.
  • Socket = IP + port, uniquely identifies a process Internet-wide.
  • The port number is 16 bits; below 1024 are "well-known" ports (HTTP is port 80, POP3 is port 110); above 1024 are dynamic.
  • NAT: use one (or a few) public IP addresses + different port numbers to map multiple internal hosts.
  • Advantage: extends the IP address space; (implicitly) hides the internal source addresses.
  • Disadvantage: a DoS attack is still feasible; it breaks end-to-end transparency.
  • Example: internal 192.168.0.12:1025 ↔ public 11.0.0.1:4000, with the NAT table maintaining the mapping.
  • ⚔ Ping flood / Ping of Death: abuse the ping command (ICMP echo request/reply); a large volume of ICMP packets overwhelms the victim; before you PoD a host, you may saturate your own bandwidth first.

docs.title: 2.6 Link layer ★
docs.text:
• Implemented in the adapter, the Network Interface Card (NIC); the NIC is "semi-autonomous" and (mostly) out of the host's control; it implements both the link and physical layers.
  • MAC address: 48 bits, globally unique; used to forward packets over one link.
  • Analogy: an IP address is like your home address, a MAC address is like a social security number.
  • ARP: given an IP address, find the corresponding MAC address; each host has an ARP table, or ARP cache, which is generated automatically and whose entries expire after about 20 min; ARP is stateless.
  • ⚔ ARP cache poisoning:
  • The attacker actively sends a forged ARP reply ("the MAC address of 111.111.111.002 is CC-CC-...");
  • Both caches are poisoned → traffic goes through the attacker → man-in-the-middle.
  • Defense: static ARP, DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection), encryption (not covered in the slides).

docs.title: 2.7 Attack surface summarized by layer ★
docs.text: Layer Attack Root cause Defense direction Application SMTP spoofing No sender authentication SPF/DKIM/DMARC Application DNS poisoning Caching + no signatures DNSSEC, randomization Application Cookie privacy Cross-site tracking Privacy policy, isolation Transport SYN flood TCP is stateful SYN cookies, rate limiting Network IP spoofing, Ping flood No source authentication, ICMP abuse Ingress filtering, rate limiting Link ARP poisoning ARP is stateless and unauthenticated Static ARP, DAI

docs.title: Example 1: Password entropy (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: For an 8-character password chosen at random from 26 lowercase letters, from 95 printable characters, and from 256 bytes respectively, what is the entropy in bits in each case? Why is the actual strength far below this?

Solution: - 26⁸: \(8\times\log_2(26) \approx 8\times4.70 = 37.6\ \text{bit}\) - 95⁸: \(8\times\log_2(95) \approx 8\times6.57 = 52.6\ \text{bit}\) - 256⁸: \(8\times8 = 64\ \text{bit}\) - In practice users do not choose at random and use dictionary words/mutations → the attacker uses a dictionary attack, and the actual search space is far smaller than the theoretical value.

docs.title: Example 2: Salting (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: The dictionary size is 10⁸ and the system has 10⁴ users. With no salt and with salt (an independent salt per user), what order of magnitude does the attacker need to crack all passwords offline in each case?

Solution: - No salt: precompute 10⁸ hashes, shared by all users → 10⁸. - With salt: every user and every salt must be recomputed → 10⁸ × 10⁴ = 10¹². - If a slow hash is added on top (0.1 second each), the cost is multiplied by the time factor.

docs.title: Example 3: EER (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: After a fingerprint system raises its threshold, fraud drops to 1% and insult rises to 10%. Explain why, and explain the meaning of EER.

Solution: - A higher threshold = harder to pass → an impostor is less likely to be accepted (fraud↓), but a legitimate user is also more likely to be rejected (insult↑). - The two trade off as the threshold changes; EER is the point where fraud=insult, used to compare different biometrics/systems (the smaller the better).

docs.title: Example 4: SYN flood (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: Describe the process of a SYN flood. Why is the root cause "TCP is stateful"?

Solution: 1. The attacker sends a large number of SYN packets (the source IP can be spoofed); 2. The server allocates a half-open connection (a backlog table entry) for each SYN and replies with SYN-ACK; 3. The attacker does not reply with ACK → the table entries are used up; 4. New legitimate SYN packets cannot enter the queue → denial of service. - Root cause: the server must remember the state of every half-open connection; state resources are limited. - Defense: SYN cookies (store no state, encode the information into the sequence number), rate limiting, shorter timeouts.

docs.title: Example 5: DNS poisoning (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: How can an attacker make a user who visits www.bank.com be directed to the attacker's own server?

Solution: 1. The attacker sends a forged response (matching the query ID/port) to the recursive DNS server, claiming that the A record of www.bank.com is the attacker's IP; 2. The recursive server caches the false record (within the TTL); 3. After that, every user who queries that domain name receives the false IP; 4. The user connects to the attacker's server (which can phish/act as a man-in-the-middle). - Defense: DNSSEC (signatures), randomizing the query ID/port, limiting caching.

docs.title: Example 6: ARP poisoning (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: How can an attacker become a man-in-the-middle between Alice and the gateway on the same LAN?

Solution: 1. The attacker sends Alice a forged ARP reply: "the MAC address of the gateway IP is my MAC"; 2. It sends the gateway a forged ARP reply: "the MAC address of Alice's IP is my MAC"; 3. Both ARP caches are poisoned, and all traffic is sent to the attacker; 4. The attacker forwards (or tampers with) the traffic → man-in-the-middle. - Root cause: ARP is stateless and unauthenticated; the cache is updated as soon as a reply arrives. - Defense: static ARP, DAI, port security.

docs.title: Example 7: NAT table (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: The internal host 192.168.0.12:1025 accesses 12.0.0.1:80; the NAT public address is 11.0.0.1 and the mapped port is 4000. Write down the source/destination addresses before and after NAT.

Solution: - Outbound: src=192.168.0.12:1025, dst=12.0.0.1:80 → src=11.0.0.1:4000, dst=12.0.0.1:80; - NAT table: 4000 ↔ 192.168.0.12:1025; - Return direction: src=12.0.0.1:80, dst=11.0.0.1:4000 → src=12.0.0.1:80, dst=192.168.0.12:1025.

docs.title: 4. Common pitfalls (where marks are easiest to lose)
docs.text: Mistake Correct Authentication = authorization Authentication confirms identity; authorization decides permissions 2FA = two passwords It must be two different categories of factors (know/have/are) A longer password is always stronger Predictable user choice destroys entropy; P@ssw0rd! is still in the dictionary Hashing a password makes it safe Without salt you can precompute/compare in bulk; you need salt + a slow hash The salt must be kept secret The salt does not need to be secret, it only needs to be unique/random A biometric can "change the password" Biometrics cannot be revoked; once leaked they cannot be replaced fraud = the genuine user is rejected fraud = the impostor is accepted; insult = the genuine user is rejected (the slides label them the other way round; memorize by definition) TCP is a "true connection" It is only a logical connection; the underlying layer is still packets UDP is unreliable, so it is useless DNS, video, games, etc. use UDP to gain low latency NAT prevents DoS NAT does not prevent DoS; it only extends addresses/hides the source ARP is a layer-3 protocol ARP sits between the link layer and the network layer and maps IP→MAC DNS has only 13 physical servers There are 13 root server clusters (multiple anycast instances) Cookie is an authentication mechanism It is only state management; its authentication power is very weak

docs.title: 5. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between authentication and authorization? Give three examples for each of the three authentication factors.
  2. Why is a 64-bit random key stronger than an 8-character password? What affects the entropy of a password?
  3. What is a dictionary attack? Why is it more effective than brute force?
  4. What advantage does a passphrase have over a "complex password"? What did the slide experiment show?
  5. What is wrong with hashed passwords without salt? How does salt fix it? Does the salt need to be kept secret?
  6. What are the four ideal properties of a biometric? What is the difference between enrollment and recognition?
  7. What are fraud and insult respectively? What is the meaning of EER?
  8. Why is "biometrics cannot be revoked" a fundamental problem?
  9. Draw the five-layer protocol stack and give two protocols for each layer.
  10. What is encapsulation? Up to which layer does a router process a packet?
  11. Why does HTTP need cookies? What is the privacy risk of cookies?
  12. How is SMTP spoofed? What are the steps of DNS cache poisoning?
  13. What is the TCP three-way handshake? What is the root cause of a SYN flood and how do you defend against it?
  14. What makes up a socket? What are the advantages and disadvantages of NAT?
  15. How does ARP poisoning create a man-in-the-middle? How do you mitigate it?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. Authentication confirms "who you are"; authorization decides "what you can do". Know: password/PIN/date of birth; have: smartcard/token/cell phone; are: fingerprint/face/voiceprint.
  2. A key is generated at random, so it has full entropy; a password is chosen by a person and is affected by dictionaries/patterns/reuse, so its actual entropy is far below the theoretical value for its length.
  3. Try only the most likely candidates (dictionary words, mutations); because user choices follow patterns, the hit rate is high, far better than brute-forcing \(2^{64}\).
  4. Longer, easy to remember, and unlikely to be hit by a dictionary; in the experiment, the passphrase group had a 10% crack rate and was easy to remember, while the complex-rule group had 30%.
  5. Precomputation, the same hash for the same password, and bulk cracking; the salt makes each user's hash unique, so the attacker must recompute user by user; the salt does not need to be secret.
  6. Universal, Distinguishing, Permanent, Collectable (+ safe/friendly). Enrollment is putting the info into the database (may be slow, must be precise); Recognition is the actual detection (must be quick and accurate).
  7. fraud: the impostor is accepted; insult: the genuine user is rejected. EER is the point where the two are equal, used to compare systems, the smaller the better.
  8. A leaked password can be changed, but a fingerprint/iris cannot be replaced; once leaked it is unusable for life.
  9. Application (HTTP/SMTP), transport (TCP/UDP), network (IP/BGP), link (Ethernet/ARP), physical.
  10. Each layer adds a header, with the application data on the inside; a router processes up to the network layer.
  11. HTTP is stateless, so cookies are used for sessions/shopping carts/recommendations; cross-site tracking and privacy leaks; weak authentication power.
  12. SMTP's MAIL FROM can be written arbitrarily; DNS poisoning: forged response → the recursive server caches the false record → the wrong IP is returned.
  13. SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK; the server keeps state for half-open connections, and when the table is full it denies service; defense: SYN cookies, rate limiting, shorter timeouts.
  14. IP + port; NAT extends addresses and hides the internal network, but it breaks end-to-end and DoS is still feasible.
  15. Forged ARP replies poison both caches so traffic goes through the attacker; defense: static ARP, DAI, port security.

docs.text: Item Content Access control Authentication (who you are) + authorization (what you can do) Three factors know / have / are 2FA Any two categories of factors Key vs password \(2^{64}\) vs user choice → dictionary attack Password experiment Complex rules 30%; passphrase 10% and easy to remember; random 10% and hard to remember salt Random, not secret, unique per user; attack volume × number of users Biometrics Universal/Distinguishing/Permanent/Collectable fraud/insult Impostor accepted / genuine user rejected; EER is the equal point Five layers application/transport/network/link/physical Encapsulation Each layer adds a header, data is on the inside HTTP Stateless; cookies add state; weak authentication; privacy SMTP Plaintext commands; MAIL FROM can be spoofed DNS 13 root clusters; cache poisoning TCP Reliable/in-order/flow control/connection-oriented; 20B header; three-way handshake SYN flood Half-open connections exhaust the backlog; the root cause is statefulness IP/socket 32-bit IP; IP + 16-bit port NAT Address reuse; hides the internal network; does not prevent DoS MAC/ARP 48-bit MAC; ARP cache ~20 min; can be poisoned
